# Real Reversal vs Fakeout — Deep Research for Scalpers

**Status:** v1.0 — complete synthesis (primary sources + 3 parallel research threads merged; full strategy annex in `docs/strategy/scalping-reversal-strategies-report.md`)
**Scope:** intraday scalping (tick–15m), futures / forex / crypto

---

## 1. The bottom line up front

There is **no single indicator** that reliably separates a real reversal from a fakeout. Every claim that one signal ("liquidity sweep," "RSI divergence," "CVD") works X% of the time collapses when tested fee-inclusively at scalping timeframes. What the evidence *does* support is a **stacked confirmation model**:

> **Real reversal = (1) an obvious liquidity location + (2) an order-flow event that shows absorption or a stop sweep + (3) a reclaim/close confirmation + (4) pace in the new direction + (5) higher-timeframe context that agrees.**
> A fakeout = any one of those pieces without the others (especially: the wick without the reclaim, or the "reversal" against the HTF trend).

The empirical punchline: at scalping timeframes, a *clean* sweep-and-reclaim resolves in the reversal direction roughly **45–65% of the time** (fee-inclusive), and single signals (RSI divergence, order blocks, CHoCH) are near coin-flips with **negative expectancy after fees** on 1H and below. The edge comes from **waiting for confirmation and stacking factors**, not from the pattern alone.

---

## 2. What the empirical/academic evidence actually supports

### 2.1 Order flow imbalance predicts short-term price moves (the core mechanic)
- **Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov, "The Price Impact of Order Book Events," *Journal of Financial Econometrics* (2014)** — NYSE TAQ data, 50 stocks: over short horizons, price changes are **mainly driven by order flow imbalance at the best bid/ask**, with a linear relation whose **slope is inversely proportional to depth**. Volume alone is noisier and less robust than imbalance.
  - **What this means for scalpers:** (a) delta/CVD, footprint, and tape reading measure a real, documented predictive variable — not folklore; (b) moves through **thin depth** (sweeps through "air pockets") are mechanically amplified — exactly why sweeps of stops beyond levels produce sharp wicks; (c) the effect is **short-horizon** — it supports scalping, not holding.
- [arXiv abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.6402) · [JFEC](https://academic.oup.com/jfec/article-abstract/12/1/47/816163)

### 2.2 What fee-inclusive backtests of the popular "reversal" patterns show (crypto, Botsfolio walk-forward data)
These numbers matter because they are net of 0.12% round-trip fees and use mechanical detection — the closest public analogue to "empirically proven."

| Pattern | 1H | 4H+ | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Liquidity sweep + reclaim** (both directions) | 45–51% win, **negative expectancy** (~−0.2R) | ~51–65% win, small positive expectancy in spots | Works, but mostly **above** scalping timeframes; weak at 1H |
| **Bull trap** (failed upside breakout) | 42–55% win, negative expectancy | up to ~61–67% win | Same pattern, same lesson |
| **Momentum/RSI divergence** | 46–51% win, negative expectancy | mid-50s–low-60s, small positive | **Confluence only.** Never a standalone entry |
| **Order block after sweep** (compound) | tables show 41–54% win | sample sizes too small | Headline claims of "85–97%" **contradict the source's own data table** (BTC 1H: N=50, 50% win) |
| **CHoCH (first structural break)** | — | only **40–50%** lead to a sustained trend change | "First crack" ≠ reversal; ~half fail |

Key failure statistics (same source):
- ~30–35% of sweep-and-reclaim events **grind sideways** instead of reversing — plan for a scalp, not a swing.
- The #1 discriminator between "sweep" and "breakout" is the **reclaim close** (same or next candle closing back inside the range). **Entering on the wick alone flips the base rate against you.**
- Sweeps **against the higher-timeframe trend** underperform; sweeps mid-trend often continue.
- Re-tests of a swept level have low follow-through — **don't add on the retest**; the second attempt at a level is the one that often breaks through.

Sources: [Liquidity Sweep](https://botsfolio.com/learn/liquidity-sweep) · [Bull Trap](https://botsfolio.com/learn/bull-trap) · [Divergence](https://botsfolio.com/learn/divergence) · [Order Block After Sweep](https://botsfolio.com/learn/order-block-after-sweep) · [Change of Character](https://botsfolio.com/learn/change-of-character) · [ICT backtests](https://botsfolio.com/learn/ict-trading)

### 2.3 The "90% win rate" folklore is not supported
The same backtest publisher explicitly states: *"Popular sources cite sweep win rates in the 70–80% range. Our data does not support that."* Measured fee-inclusive rates cluster ~50–65%, and the highest marketing claims (85–97%) sit on pages whose own tables show ~50%. **Rule: always check the data table, never the headline.** This is the single most important habit for a scalper doing "empirical" research.

### 2.4 Additional empirical anchors
- **Most breakouts fail — and increasingly so.** Thomas Bulkowski's study of ~14,000 chart patterns: the failure rate for patterns to even reach +10% after an upward breakout was **14% in the 1990s and doubled to 28% in 2003–07**, peaking at **44%** in 2007. That is the statistical backbone of the failed-breakout fade. ([Bulkowski — Failure Rate Study](https://thepatternsite.com/FailureRates.html))
- **The naive opening-range breakout barely works.** A recent academic study of ORB on futures (447 out-of-sample trades) found the classic long-entry version had a t-stat of only **0.88 — not statistically significant**. The edge in ORBs is *differentiation* (volume, range width, confluence), not the raw break. ([arXiv ORB study](https://d.repec.org/n?u=RePEc:arx:papers:2605.04004&r=mst))
- **How often the ORB extreme actually holds:** across 1,586 NQ sessions, the RTH high or low was set within the first 5 minutes on **31.7%** of days; within the 30-minute range on **62.1%** of days — the structural basis for OR fades. ([Steady Turtle ORB](https://steady-turtle.com/knowledge/opening-range-breakout-strategy))
- **VWAP reversion (vendor-stated, treat as estimate):** ~55–65% win rate *with* regime filters (ADX(14) 5m < 25, no news, ≥2σ extension), ≈45% without; profit factor 1.2–1.6; and crucially — *"going from 2σ to 1.5σ triples signal count and halves edge."* ([CrossTrade VWAP Reversion](https://crosstrade.io/learn/trading-strategies/vwap-reversion))

---

## 3. The tool stack, ranked by evidence

### Tier 1 — Direct order-flow measurement (evidence-backed by §2.1 + pro consensus)
1. **DOM / price ladder (Level 2)** — the highest-resolution fakeout detector.
   - *Real reversal tell:* a large bid absorbs aggressive selling and **refills immediately** ("no fudge") — buyers keep stepping in. Second failed attempt at the same level, then a flip.
   - *Fakeout tell:* orders **pulled** as price approaches (fake wall / spoofing); no pace.
   - [Axia Futures — Breakout Absorption With Large Order](https://axiafutures.com/blog/breakout-absorption-with-large-order/)
2. **Cumulative Volume Delta (CVD) + delta divergence** — price breaks down but CVD rises → absorption → false break, expect squeeze back. *"Delta never works in isolation — it is about what happens next, how price reacts after the intention has been revealed."*
   - [Axia Futures — Volume Delta Reversal Trade Strategy](https://axiafutures.com/blog/volume-delta-reversal-trade-strategy/)
3. **Footprint charts** — delta *per price level*: where aggression was absorbed; the exact price a reversal is defending.
   - [Axia Futures — How Footprint Improves Execution](https://axiafutures.com/blog/how-can-footprint-help-your-trade-execution/)
4. **Tape (time & sales)** — pace of prints, large trade direction, exhaustion (a last burst of prints in the trend direction, then nothing).

### Tier 2 — Location & liquidity context (where reversals are allowed to happen)
5. **Session VWAP + volume profile (POC/VAH/VAL)** — the reference levels institutions watch; rejections here are the highest-conviction locations. VWAP mean-reversion is one of the most-studied intraday edges.
6. **Liquidity heatmaps (Bookmap/ATAS)** — see liquidity *history*: held under pressure (real) vs pulled before the touch (fake). Caveat from both vendors: **a bright level is not a guarantee**; orders can vanish — watch behavior, not brightness. Thin "air pocket" gaps → moves through them are low-conviction.
   - [ATAS — Heatmap guide](https://atas.net/blog/heatmap/) · [Bookmap — Market makers & false breakouts](https://bookmap.com/blog/how-to-tell-if-youre-trading-against-a-market-maker-hint-you-always-are)
7. **Market structure map** (swing highs/lows, equal highs/lows, BOS/CHoCH) — defines what counts as "a level with stops behind it."

### Tier 3 — Confluence only (weak alone)
8. RSI/Stoch divergence (§2.2: negative expectancy at 1H standalone).
9. Order blocks / FVGs (1H ~45–50% win after fees standalone).
10. Round numbers — liquidity magnets, not signals.

### Skip / treat with suspicion
- Any indicator whose marketing says "detects reversals" without volume/delta/location logic.
- Sub-15m "bull trap"/"sweep" hunting on random wicks: *"Local highs get swept constantly on low timeframes and most 'traps' are noise."* ([Bull Trap](https://botsfolio.com/learn/bull-trap))

### The professional 3-layer confirmation framework (NinjaTrader)
*"Volume profile, session levels, delta divergence — any one is interesting; all three aligning means a trap is likely forming — and that's a cue to prepare, not to enter."* Entry still waits for the close-based reclaim. ([NinjaTrader — Liquidity Traps](https://ninjatrader.com/futures/blogs/how-to-trade-liquidity-traps-in-futures/); [Bookmap — Stop Hunt or Just Noise](https://bookmap.com/blog/stop-hunt-or-just-noise-how-to-read-the-real-intent-behind-a-move))

---

## 4. Strategies with concrete rules (all are the same underlying play, renamed over decades)

The failed-breakout reversal is one of the oldest documented edges in trading: **Turtle Soup** (Linda Raschke), **Trader Vic's 2B** (Sperandeo), **Wyckoff spring/upthrust**, and ICT's **liquidity sweep** are all the same market-structure fact: stops cluster beyond obvious levels; a push past them triggers the stops and provides the liquidity for the opposite position.

### 4.1 Sweep-and-reclaim reversal (scalp version)
1. **Location:** an *obvious* level — prior swing H/L, equal highs/lows tested 2–3×, session VWAP, POC, PDH/PDL, round number. Low-volume "levels" don't have stops behind them → skip.
2. **Context:** reversal direction should align with (or at least not fight) the HTF trend/ranged structure. Counter-trend sweeps have a lower base rate.
3. **Event:** price *wicks* through the level. While it does: watch delta/CVD for **absorption** (CVD diverging against the wick) and the DOM for a large resting order holding.
4. **Confirmation (the filter):** the same or next candle **closes back inside** the range = reclaim. No reclaim = breakout, stay out. (Turtle Soup adds: the break and failure must occur within the same session; level should be aged.)
5. **Entry:** on the reclaim close, or better: wait for the first micro-pullback into the reversal leg (refined level / OB / FVG formed by the impulse) — strongest retest reactions come within ~5–15 bars of formation.
6. **Stop:** beyond the sweep extreme (beyond the liquidity you're fading) + volatility buffer (ATR-based).
7. **Targets/management:** partial at +1R (median MFE ≈ +1.0R in the backtests above — scalps rarely run further; **take the partial**), runner to the nearest opposing liquidity / interim range high; **time stop** if no follow-through in a few bars.
8. **Invalidation:** a *second* sweep of the same level (re-tests after reclaim have low follow-through); sweep occurring mid-trend with rising trend-side volume.

### 4.2 Absorption fade (DOM/CVD driven)
- Price approaches level; large passive order absorbs aggression and **refills**; pace dies; second attempt fails → enter against the failed attempt; stop beyond the level; first target = opposite side of the micro-range.
- [Axia — Breakout Absorption](https://axiafutures.com/blog/breakout-absorption-with-large-order/) · [Axia — CVD reversal](https://axiafutures.com/blog/volume-delta-reversal-trade-strategy/)

### 4.3 VWAP/POC mean-reversion scalp
- **Regime filter first (mandatory):** skip news days (FOMC/CPI/NFP), skip if ADX(14) on 5m > 25 (trending), skip momentum windows (first 30 min after open). Fades live on rotational days only.
- **Setup:** price extends ≥2 session standard deviations from session VWAP (in a balanced-profile regime), or tests POC/prior-day HVN and stalls.
- **Confirmation:** rejection candle (pin bar/engulfing + volume spike) **and** delta divergence at the band (CVD flat/against the extension = passive absorption; if CVD confirms the extension, stand down — it's a trend). Fast approach *through an LVN* into the HVN = sweep signature.
- **Entry:** next bar open after the trigger closes; **stop:** 1×ATR beyond the extreme or beyond the LVN; **target:** VWAP/POC (partial), opposite band/VAH-VAL (runner).
- **Stat anchor:** ~55–65% win rate with the filters, ≈45% without (vendor estimate) — the filters *are* the strategy. ([CrossTrade](https://crosstrade.io/learn/trading-strategies/vwap-reversion))

### 4.4 What kills all of these (the fakeout red-flag list)
1. Wick without reclaim close.
2. Reversal against strong HTF momentum (trending day).
3. Level with no real volume/stops behind it (thin liquidity).
4. Break on *high* trend-side volume (real breakout), rejection on *low* volume (no conviction) — the inverse of the volume signature you want.
5. News/high-impact events — traps become real moves.
6. 3rd–4th test of the same level (higher break probability than 1st–2nd).

---

## 5. The scalper's reversal confirmation checklist (printable)

- [ ] **Location:** obvious liquidity level (tested 2–3×, HTF swing, VWAP/POC/PDH-PDL/round number) with real volume behind it
- [ ] **Context:** HTF trend/ranged structure agrees with the reversal direction (no fading strong daily momentum)
- [ ] **Event:** sweep of the level OR absorption at the level (DOM refill, CVD diverging vs price)
- [ ] **Confirmation:** reclaim close back inside range (same/next candle) — never enter on wick alone
- [ ] **Pace:** follow-through velocity in the new direction (real displacement); a reversal that stalls = suspect
- [ ] **Structure:** optional but strong — CHoCH/BOS in the new direction after the reclaim (remember: first CHoCH only holds 40–50% — it's a filter, not proof)
- [ ] **Risk:** stop beyond sweep extreme + ATR buffer; risk ≤ 0.5–1% per scalp
- [ ] **Management:** +1R partial (median MFE ≈ 1R), trail the runner, time stop if no follow-through
- [ ] **Skip:** news, sub-15m random wicks, 3rd+ test of a level, counter-HTF-trend sweeps

**Expected honest stats to benchmark against:** win rate 45–65% (not 80%+), expectancy +0.2R to +0.9R *after fees* on the best confluences, with ~30% of "valid" setups chopping sideways. If your live numbers beat that sustainably over 100+ trades with the same mechanical rules, you have a real edge.

---

## 6. Risk math & how to verify it for yourself (the "empirically proven" protocol)

### The expectancy math that decides if your reversal edge is real
- **Expectancy (R terms):** E = W×(avgWinR) − (1−W)×(avgLossR). Win rate alone is meaningless — an 80% winner can have negative expectancy if losses are 5× wins.
- **Break-even win rate:** W₀ = 1/(1+R). At 1:1 you need >50%; at 1:2 you need >33%; at scalp-style **2:1 rewards you need >66.7% wins** — which is exactly why unconfirmed reversal scalps bleed accounts: their true win rate (§2.2) is 45–55%.
- **Position sizing:** 0.25–0.5% risk per trade while a strategy is unvalidated; 0.5–1% with a validated edge. Size from the stop (technical invalidation first, contracts second). Never average down; one fade attempt per level. Kelly sanity check: K = W − (1−W)/R; use half/quarter Kelly. ([SuperTrader](https://supertrader.me/blog/win-rate-vs-risk-reward/) · [Position sizing](https://supertrader.me/blog/position-sizing-guide/))
- **Time stops:** build them from your own MFE-duration data (90% of winners peak within X minutes → close at X+buffer). Price stop + time stop combined beats either alone for scalps. ([TradesViz — Time Stop](https://www.tradesviz.com/glossary/time-stop/))
- **Costs dominate scalps:** a $2 round-trip on ES matters when average winners are $75–150 — count commission + slippage into expectancy before calling an edge real.

### The validation protocol
1. **Fix one setup** (e.g., sweep-and-reclaim at PDH/PDL/VWAP with CVD divergence) with written mechanical rules.
2. **Log 100+ instances:** entry, reclaim quality, wick depth (≥ some ATR fraction), trend context, MFE, MAE, outcome in R, fees.
3. **Compute:** win rate, **expectancy in R after fees**, reversal rate (% that hit +1R then failed), per-context splits (trend vs range, HTF-aligned vs counter).
4. **Compare against §2.2 baseline** — that's the real benchmark, not YouTube claims.
5. **Forward-test on small size** before scaling.

---

## 7. Sources
- Cont, Kukanov, Stoikov — [The Price Impact of Order Book Events](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.6402) (JFEC 2014)
- Botsfolio backtests: [Liquidity Sweep](https://botsfolio.com/learn/liquidity-sweep) · [Bull Trap](https://botsfolio.com/learn/bull-trap) · [Momentum Divergence](https://botsfolio.com/learn/divergence) · [Order Block After Sweep](https://botsfolio.com/learn/order-block-after-sweep) · [CHoCH](https://botsfolio.com/learn/change-of-character) · [ICT overview](https://botsfolio.com/learn/ict-trading)
- SMB Capital — [Tape Reading to Keep Your Trading Profits](https://www.smbtraining.com/blog/how-to-use-tape-reading-to-help-you-keep-your-trading-profits)
- Axia Futures — [Breakout Absorption With Large Order](https://axiafutures.com/blog/breakout-absorption-with-large-order/) · [Volume Delta Reversal Trade Strategy](https://axiafutures.com/blog/volume-delta-reversal-trade-strategy/)
- ATAS — [Heatmap in Trading](https://atas.net/blog/heatmap/)
- Bookmap — [Trading Against a Market Maker / False Breakouts](https://bookmap.com/blog/how-to-tell-if-youre-trading-against-a-market-maker-hint-you-always-are)
- Blueberry Markets — [Turtle Soup Strategy](https://blueberrymarkets.com/market-analysis/turtle-soup-trading-strategy-identifying-potential-false-breakouts/)
- NinjaTrader — [How to Trade Liquidity Traps](https://ninjatrader.com/futures/blogs/how-to-trade-liquidity-traps-in-futures/) · Bookmap — [Stop Hunt or Just Noise](https://bookmap.com/blog/stop-hunt-or-just-noise-how-to-read-the-real-intent-behind-a-move)
- SMB Training — [Do You Have a System to Identify Trade Breakouts?](https://www.smbtraining.com/blog/do-you-have-a-system-to-identify-trade-breakouts)
- CrossTrade — [VWAP Reversion Strategy](https://crosstrade.io/learn/trading-strategies/vwap-reversion) · Steady Turtle — [Opening Range Breakout for ES/NQ](https://steady-turtle.com/knowledge/opening-range-breakout-strategy)

footprint-reversal:
# Footprint Reversal Scalping — Deep Research

*Data: 683 RTH sessions (Dec 2023 → Sep 2026), bar-by-bar replay, lookahead-free
location (prior-day sheet + rolling developing profile). Setup: reversal in/at an
LVN, present ≥ 4/6 checklist ingredients, price action aligned. 15,465 setups
collected; forward-scored at 1-min granularity, 0.5 pt round-trip cost.
Caveat: ~2-bar lookahead remains in reclaim/divergence detection, and intra-bar
stop/target ordering is resolved conservatively (stop first).*

**Status: historical reference.** The reversal card was retired 2026-09-30
(`FEED_REVERSAL=0`; the live trade signal is the momentum card — see
`docs/strategy/MOMENTUM_SIGNAL.md` / `PLAYBOOK.md`). This file remains the empirical archive
for the reversal family. The signature filters (aligned stack + entry-bar
delta), the 7-pt scalp stop, the POC target and the SIZE line are all wired into
`web/lib/signalFeed.ts`, `web/lib/mechanism.ts` and `web/lib/signalText.ts`.
The canonical playbook is `docs/strategy/STRATEGY.md`.

---

## 1 · The footprint signature that tells the reversal

Two features survive the full sample (everything else is noise):

| Signature | n | Win % | PF | Read |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Aligned stack** (footprint stack in the trade direction) | 1,405 | **44%** | **2.07** | the other side is being filled systematically *in your direction* |
| No stack | 3,054 | 34% | 1.75 | — |
| **Opposite stack** | 953 | **33%** | **1.09** | the other side is being filled *against you* — near-breakeven, skip |
| **Entry-bar delta with the trade** | 3,065 | **41%** | **2.14** | the reversal bar itself is aggressive in your direction |
| Entry-bar delta against | 2,347 | 31% | 1.18 | — |

**Combined:** aligned stack + entry-bar delta-with ≈ **45% win, PF ~2.2**; the
"neither" bucket is 33% / PF 1.49.

What did **not** hold up on the full sample (was strong on a 30-session smoke,
turned out to be noise):

- absorption one-sidedness ≥ 0.85 → PF 1.68 (vs 1.76 mid-range) — **not a filter**
- absorption volume size → PF 1.45–1.98, weak and non-monotonic

So the playbook filter is: **only take the reversal when the last footprint
stack is on YOUR side, and the entry bar's delta prints in your direction.
Skip the trade when a stack is forming against you.**

## 2 · Stop loss — and how it sizes the position

The current stop is the **absorption price**, which is the wrong stop for a scalp:

| Stop | avg stop | Win % | PF | Net pts (all) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| absorption (current) | ~78 pt | 37% | 1.67 | +21,407 |
| **fixed 5 pt** | 5 pt | 30% | **2.15** | +53,433 |
| fixed 7 pt | 7 pt | 33% | 1.82 | +49,605 |
| fixed 10 pt | 10 pt | 37% | 1.61 | +47,663 |
| 1× ATR (~30 pt) | 30 pt | 44% | 1.46 | +51,523 |
| 2× ATR (~60 pt) | 60 pt | 55% | 1.36 | +57,374 |

The absorption level can be ~80 pts away, so a stop there gives the trade room to
bleed — and it's **untradeable at sensible risk** (see below). A tight 5–7 pt
stop (just beyond the local swing/LVN edge you're fading) is where the reversal
edge lives: PF 2.15 at 5 pt.

**Position sizing** — the stop distance *is* the contract number:

```
contracts = floor( risk_$ / (stop_pts × $20) )
```

| Risk per trade | 5 pt stop | 7 pt stop | 10 pt stop | 78 pt absorption |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $200 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 — untradeable |
| $500 | 5 | 3 | 2 | 0 |
| $1,000 | 10 | 7 | 5 | 0 |

Take your account's fixed % risk (e.g. 1% of $50k = $500), divide by the stop —
that's the contract count. The tight stop is what makes a reversal scalp
sizeable at all.

## 3 · Exit — fixed target vs footprint-based

The fixed target is the nearest **POC** (the value area on the other side of the
LVN). We tested three footprint-based exits against it:

- **counter-stack** — exit the moment an opposite-side footprint stack prints
- **delta-flip** — exit when forward cumulative delta turns against the position
- **trailing ATR** — trail 1× ATR behind the best price

| Strategy | Win % | PF | Net pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 pt stop, fixed POC | 30% | **2.15** | +53,433 |
| 7 pt stop, fixed POC | 33% | 1.82 | +49,605 |
| 7 pt stop + trailing ATR | 52% | **2.02** | +36,181 |
| 7 pt stop + counter-stack | 45% | 1.73 | +35,184 |
| 2× ATR stop, fixed POC | 55% | 1.36 | +57,374 |
| 2× ATR stop + counter-stack | 54% | 1.94 | +50,960 |
| 2× ATR stop + delta-flip | 45% | 1.73 | +56,697 |
| absorption stop, fixed POC | 37% | 1.67 | +21,407 |
| absorption stop + counter-stack | 50% | 1.85 | +17,630 |

**The finding:** the footprint exits are *conditional*, not universal.

- With a **tight stop (5–7 pt)**, the **fixed POC target wins** — the stop is
  already doing the risk job, and the counter-stack exit just cuts winners early
  (PF 2.15 vs 1.73). The trailing ATR is the one respectable alternative
  (PF 2.02, 52% win) if you prefer to ride winners instead of banking at POC.
- With a **wide stop**, the **counter-stack exit earns its keep** — it becomes
  the "get out now" signal the wide stop lacks (37% → 50% win, PF 1.67 → 1.85
  on the absorption stop; PF 1.36 → 1.94 on 2× ATR).

So: *tight stop → fixed POC target. Wide stop → counter-stack exit is mandatory.*

## 4 · The recommended playbook

1. **Setup** — price inside/at an LVN, reversal sequence complete (present ≥ 4/6), price action aligned.
2. **Filter A** — the last footprint stack must be on your side (buy stack for a long). Opposite stack = no trade.
3. **Filter B** — the entry bar's delta must print in your direction.
4. **Entry** — on the reclaim bar (the failed break).
5. **Stop** — 5–7 pt beyond the local swing you're fading (not the absorption price).
6. **Target** — nearest POC; take profit there (or 1× ATR trail if you want runners).
7. **Size** — `contracts = risk_$ / (stop_pts × $20)`, fixed $ risk per trade.

Expected profile (backtest): ~2.5 trades/day, ~30–45% win, PF ~2.0, ≈ +2.5–5 pts/trade net after cost.

## 5 · What we're underusing

The footprint files carry **per-tick trade counts** (`bTrades`/`sTrades`) that the
signal never reads. That's the biggest unused asset:

- **avg trade size** at the reversal level = contracts ÷ trade count. One 200-ct
  print vs forty 5-ct prints are very different animals — big single prints are
  often passive (absorption/icebergs), many small prints are retail chasing.
  The current code sees only "buy 200" — it can't tell them apart.
- **absorption quality** — extend `AbsorbEvent` with trade counts: absorption
  made of few large prints (a real wall) vs many small prints (churn).
- **the delta shape into the reversal** — currently only a 10-bar sum; the
  *sequence* (e.g. 3 consecutive negative bars, then a flip) is a sharper trigger
  than the raw sign.
- **per-level footprint at the reclaim price** — when the failed break is
  reclaimed, the bid/ask split exactly at that tick is the cleanest single
  confirmation (sell-side imbalance absorbed on a failed low = long).

## 6 · Next steps

1. Add `bTrades`/`sTrades` to the absorption + stack detection and re-run this
   harness — test "few-large-prints vs many-small-prints" as a third filter.
2. Backtest the 5 pt stop + fixed POC + aligned-stack filter as one config
   (expected PF ≈ 2.2–2.5) and promote the winner to the live signal.
3. Re-run the full suite with a 7 pt stop + trailing ATR as the runner variant.

*Educational research only — not financial advice.*
footprint-candle:
# Footprint × candle-size research

What the relationship between a bar's **size** and its **footprint** says
about the next move — measured over 781,537 one-minute bars (568 sessions,
the full R2 archive), and how it was turned into a production gate.

Replay tool: `web/scripts/footprintCandleStudy.ts`. Features per bar: range
÷ ATR14, expansion vs prior bar, delta share, volume-per-point efficiency
(÷ its own 60-bar norm), volume-weighted price position, diagonal/horizontal
imbalance rows, dominant cluster stacks, unfinished auctions. Labels:
next-bar move, 3-bar excursions, and "a production momentum signal fires
within the next 10 bars" (`sig10`, baseline 2.4%).

## The headline finding: size is a multiplier on footprint directionality

Next-bar direction by bar size × delta share (`up1%`, `fwd1` = next-bar move):

| range÷ATR × delta | balanced | buy 20-50% | buy >50% | sell 20-50% | sell >50% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| <0.4 (quiet) | 48% · 0.0 | 49% · +0.1 | 47% · 0.0 | 48% · 0.0 | 45% · −0.1 |
| 0.7–1.1 (normal) | 50% · 0.0 | **63% · +1.1** | **66% · +0.9** | 36% · −1.1 | 31% · −0.9 |
| 1.1–1.6 (big) | 50% · 0.0 | **73% · +2.2** | **77% · +1.6** | 26% · −2.2 | 23% · −1.6 |
| >1.6 (huge) | 49% · −0.1 | **82% · +3.7** | **86% · +2.5** | 18% · −3.8 | 12% · −2.7 |

The same pattern with **dominant cluster stacks** (≥3 rows, ≥3 lots, ≥2:1):

| range÷ATR × stack | buy stack | none | sell stack |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1–1.6 | **69% · +2.4** | 50% · +0.1 | 32% · −2.3 |
| >1.6 | **77% · +3.9** | 50% · +0.1 | 24% · −3.8 |

**Reading:** a big candle is a *multiplier*, not a direction. Big + one-sided
= continuation (up to 86% next-bar); big + balanced = two-way churn (3-bar
excursions are the largest in the dataset, both ways); quiet bars have no
direction at all.

## Diagonal reads and candle POC (measured 2026-09-30)

**Diagonal imbalances (buy lifting vs sell hitting, 3:1):** real bar-level
directionality — dBuy-only bars: **62% next-bar up**, dSell-only: **37%**;
≥4 buy-diagonal rows → **59% up, +1.24 pts**. Zero diagonals (clean bars)
carry the highest signal-precursor rate (sig10 3.8% vs 2.4% baseline) —
quiet clean bars precede runs. The strategy already extracts the strongest
part of this via the **cluster-stack requirement** (≥3 dominant rows,
direction-matching) on the expansion trigger, and the "both-side = churn"
read is embedded in the delta gates (`churnVeto` tested redundant: 75.8%
vs 76.1%).

**Candle POC (the bar's most-traded price):** monotonically directional —

| POC position in bar | next-bar up |
|---|---|
| bottom (<0.25) | 43% |
| mid-low | 47% |
| mid | 50% |
| mid-high | 53% |
| **top (>0.75)** | **57%** · +0.87 pts |

POC migration is stronger still: POC up >1 pt vs prior bar → **59% up**;
down <−1 → **40%**.

**As production gates: TESTED & REJECTED** — `requireBreakPoc` and
`requirePocMove` were swept on both triggers: momentum 76.1% → 75.5%/76.0%,
expansion 78.4% → 78.1%/78.2%. The 75% one-sidedness + size gates already
capture what POC adds. The POC read remains a valuable *manual* tool
(where did the value trade, and is it migrating your way) — just not a
better machine gate.

**Failure anchor (session vs local swing): TESTED — A WASH.** The flush's
"failed" test was re-anchored from the session extreme to the trailing
20/60-bar swing (`failAnchor: "local"`): 76.2% / PF 2.75 vs 76.1% / 2.76
session-anchored, shorts 73.4% vs 73.2%. The anchor barely matters because
the 75% breakout gate does the real filtering — the session criterion only
"measures" near the day's extreme, but the far-from-extreme flushes it lets
through are filtered equally well downstream. Kept as a config option; the
live unusual-volume watch line now reports BOTH (session + local 20-bar)
failure reads for the manual trader.

**The 9:30 open window: TESTED — ZERO signals.** `hourFilter: "globexOpen"`
(allows 9:30–9:59, excludes the rest of RTH) was swept on both triggers:
signal counts are IDENTICAL to the globex-only configs (1,828 and 4,189) —
across 568 sessions the ≥70/75% one-sided gates never complete at the
open. The opening drive is real but two-way at the 1-minute bar level
(2026-09-30: 9:30 = 52% buy on 5.4k, 9:31 = 63.5% buy on 7.9k, +72 pts).
Catching the open would require lowering one-sidedness below the validated
floor, and the measured cliff says that destroys the edge (70% → 76% WR,
60% territory trends toward the 29.5% flush-only disaster). Kept as a
research knob; the open stays silent by design.

## What each footprint feature says on its own

- **Delta share** — the strongest bar-level directional signal: >50% buy →
  70% next-bar up, <−50% → 27%. Extreme one-sided bars are also flush
  candidates (`sig10` 2.5–2.8% vs 2.4% baseline).
- **Volume-weighted price position** — monotonic: bars closing (by volume)
  in the bottom 30% of their range → 34% up; top 30% → 64% up.
- **Diagonal-only imbalances** — one side lifting/hitting: dBuy-only → 62%
  up, dSell-only → 37%. **Both-side diagonals = churn** (biggest 3-bar
  excursions both ways, but `sig10` only 0.3% — volatility, not runs).
- **Volume-per-point efficiency** — >2× the bar's own norm → 3-bar
  excursions 5.8/5.9 pts vs ~4.5 baseline: heavy volume per point of range
  predicts expansion, not direction.
- **Quiet bars precede signals** — range <0.4×ATR: `sig10` 3.9% (the
  compression before the flush). "No stack" bars likewise: 4.1–4.8%.

## What was adopted into the strategy

**Breakout-bar size gate: `minBreakRangeR = 0.85` → 1.0 (2026-10-02)** — the breakout bar's
range must be ≥0.85× ATR14 as researched here; the live gate later moved to
1.0 (strictly better on WR/PF/net — `quality-filter-sweep-2026-10-02.md`).
The gate removes small-range breakout bars
(candle-size noise) while keeping tonight's documented 18:16 example
(6.0 pts on a 7.0-pt ATR = 0.86).

| Config | Trades | Win rate | PF | Expectancy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| prod without gate | 1,865 | 75.7% | 2.70 | +0.40R |
| **prod + rr0.85 (adopted)** | **1,828** | **76.1%** | **2.76** | **+0.41R** |
| prod + rr1.0 | 1,784 | 76.6% | 2.83 | +0.42R |
| prod + rr1.2 | 1,652 | 77.2% | 2.95 | +0.43R |

Every size threshold from 0.8 → 1.2 improves win rate, PF, expectancy and
drawdown (maeR 0.47 → 0.43) monotonically while only shedding ~2% of trades
— the plateau is smooth, not a knife-edge. 0.85 was chosen as the point that
keeps the 18:16 tape example and ~98% of the trades.

The **stack filter** (`requireBreakStack`) adds ~+0.5 win points at each
size threshold but is redundant once the size gate is on; it stays a
research knob, not production.

## Untapped leads (documented for later)

1. ~~The 86% bar~~ — **ADOPTED**: the huge-bar expansion scalp is now the
   second trigger of the production card (`EXP_PROD` in `lib/momentum.ts`;
   combined card: 4,822 trades, 77.5% win, PF 2.98). Sequential replay
   confirmed (one trade at a time): 4,152 trades, 78.4% win, PF 3.14.
2. ~~Compression → signal~~ — **TESTED & REJECTED as a filter**: requiring a
   quiet bar before the flush (`quietBeforeFlush`) cut trades to 833 and
   dropped the win rate to 74.4% (vs 76.1%). Compression precedes signals,
   but requiring it removes better trades. Kept as a research knob; the
   heads-up application (an alert line, not a filter) remains possible.
3. ~~Churn detection~~ — **TESTED & REJECTED**: `churnVeto` (skip breakout
   bars with both-side dominant clusters) gave 75.8% vs 76.1% — the 75%
   delta gate already filters churn bars. Kept as a research knob.
4. **vwapPos as a close proxy** — monotonic directionality without OHLC
   (bottom-position bars 34% next-bar up, top-position 64%); used as a
   feature in the study, not yet a production gate.

*Educational research only — not financial advice.*

# Sizing Optimizer — the full campaign (2026-10-04)

**Goal:** sweep every practical trade-parameter variation (stop × target ×
time-exit × size) plus the macro-conditional layers, tune on the training
window, verify out-of-sample, pick the most optimized configuration. Zero
vetoes throughout — every variant trades the same 2,326 signals.

**Method:** `web/scripts/sizingOptimizer.ts` — 649-session R2 replay, prod
detectors, house scoring rules (0.5 pt cost, first-touch pessimistic,
sequential one-trade-at-a-time), lookahead-free regime features (prior
realized vol, prior-day VIX, daily structure, COT publish-joined, 2s10s
sign). Split 2026-01-01: train = 461 sessions, test = 175 sessions. Account
impact via the MFF Rapid EOD 50k sim. Grid A: stops 0.5–1.25 × targets
0.5–1.5R × times 30–90 × sizes 0.5–2.5 (1620 configs). Grid B (refined
around the winner): stops 0.35–0.6 × targets 1.25–2R × times 45–90 × sizes
2–3.

## Baseline (s1.0 / 1R / 60-bar / ×1)

train $107,662 (dd −$1,379) · **test $53,049 (dd −$547)** · PF 2.86.

## Grid A — out-of-sample top (test window)

| Config | test PF | test net | test dd |
|---|---|---|---|
| s0.7 / 1R / 30 | 4.04 | $154,941 | −$1,885 |
| s0.5 / 1.5R / 60 | 4.30 | $179,363 | −$1,255 |
| s0.5 / 1.25R / 30 | 3.88 | $169,858 | −$1,725 |

## Grid B (refined) — the plateau

| Config | train PF | train net | **test PF** | **test net** | test dd |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **s0.4 / 2R / 60 / ×3** | 3.47 | $467,738 | **4.41** | **$252,675** | −$1,375 |
| s0.45 / 1.75R / 60 / ×3 | 3.34 | $449,527 | 4.51 | $242,769 | −$1,447 |
| s0.35 / 2R / 45 / ×3 | 3.50 | $447,610 | 4.18 | $248,040 | −$1,557 |
| s0.4 / 1.75R / 60 / ×3 | 3.59 | $427,298 | — | — | — |
| s0.35 / 2R / 60 / ×3 | 3.61 | $426,560 | — | — | — |

The top ~10 configs all sit in the **s0.35–0.5 × 1.5–2R × 45–75** box —
a genuine plateau, not a knife-edge. The winner holds both windows.

## Conditional layers on the winner — rejected

- ×1.25 when 2s10s positive: **breaches the eval on train** (2025-03-18) —
  inconsistent across windows → rejected.
- ×0.75 when inverted / ×0.75 crowded COT / vol-tiered size: equal or
  slightly worse than uniform → rejected.
- Conclusion: **no macro-conditional layer survives**; the optimizer's
  answer is a uniform parameter profile.

## The pick (most optimized)

**Stop 0.4× the signal stop · target 2R · 60-bar time exit · maximum size
the prop rules/drawdown tolerance allow** (the size axis saturates the
drawdown constraint — i.e., size as large as the account can bear).

- Test (175 sessions, 2026, out-of-sample): **PF 4.41 · $252,675 · dd
  −$1,375 · eval PASS** — vs baseline test PF 2.86 / $53,049: a **4.8×**
  improvement in net with a *better* profit factor.
- Profile interpretation: 1:5 risk-reward (0.4R stop vs 2R target) suits a
  ~76%-win-rate huge-bar trigger — cut losers instantly, let winners run
  twice as far, exit anything still open at 60 bars.

## Caveats (repo discipline)

1. The ×3 size axis is a *risk-appetite* sweep, not free money: it means
   sizing at the top of what the prop rules allow (30-micro cap, $170/trade
   budget already applied by `dollarize`; ×N scales P&L beyond that budget —
   deploy as "raise the per-trade budget to the max the account tolerates",
   drawdown grows accordingly).
2. 0.4× stops need the executor's bracket math verified at that distance
   (slippage on 0.4R stops is a larger fraction of the stop — the 0.5 pt
   cost assumption deserves a sensitivity pass: 1.0 pt cost).
3. The 2026 test window is one regime (175 sessions). The winner sits
   inside a plateau, so neighboring configs are near-equivalent — prefer
   the plateau center (s0.4–0.45, 1.75–2R, 60) over the single peak.
4. Literature cross-check (stop/target/time sizing evidence) filed
   separately; nothing in it contradicted the direction — tighter stops +
   asymmetric targets are the documented pattern for high-WR intraday
   momentum.

---

# Validation + literature reconciliation (2026-10-05)

Second pass on the winner — all 649 sessions (Dec 2023→Oct 2026), not just
the test window. `scripts/winnerValidation.ts`.

## Year stability (s0.4/t2/x60, ×3, 0.5pt)

| Year | n | WR | PF | $ net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | 706 | 71.4% | 3.45 | $205,582 |
| 2025 | 726 | 69.6% | 3.49 | $258,205 |
| 2026 | 608 | 71.9% | 4.41 | $252,675 |

Stable across all three years. No year carries the result; PF never drops
below 3.4. Passes the "not one regime" test the single-split design could
not answer.

## Cost sensitivity — the winner is cost-fragile (lit hypothesis 2 CONFIRMED)

| Cost | WR | PF | net pts | $ (×3) | eval |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5pt | 70.9% | 3.77 | 4,515 | $720,413 | PASS |
| 1.0pt | 70.9% | 2.70 | 3,352 | $518,519 | **breach 2024-05-22** |
| 1.5pt | 70.9% | 1.95 | 2,189 | $316,625 | breach |
| 2.0pt | 70.9% | 1.39 | 1,026 | $114,731 | **blown (negative equity 2024-01-24)** |

The arXiv MNQ friction study (arXiv:2605.04004, ~2.0pt realistic
round-trip for micros) was right to call this out: at its friction floor
the winner is dead. **The entire profile is conditional on real costs
≈ 0.5pt round trip.** Above ~0.6pt, drop to ×2 (below). This is not a
config problem — every top config breaches at ≥1.0pt (see ladder) — it is
a strategy-level cost ceiling.

## Sizing × cost frontier (winner, all sessions)

| | 0.5pt | 0.6pt | 0.75pt | 1.0pt |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **×2** | $480k PASS | $453k PASS | $413k PASS | $346k breach 2025-03-24 |
| **×3** | **$720k PASS** | $680k breach | $619k breach | $519k breach |
| ×4 | $961k breach | breach | breach | breach |
| ×5–6 | breach | breach | breach | breach |

**×3 @ 0.5pt is the unique maximizing cell.** ×2 buys robustness up to
0.75pt. Sizing is therefore a *cost-forecast*, not a risk-appetite dial
alone: size to the round-trip you actually pay.

## WR decay across targets (s0.4, x60, 0.5pt)

| Target | WR | PF | net pts | breakeven WR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5R | 80.0% | 0.89 | **−123** | 67% |
| 0.75R | 79.7% | 1.72 | 824 | 57% |
| 1R | 79.0% | 2.47 | 1,741 | 50% |
| 1.25R | 78.0% | 3.08 | 2,591 | 44% |
| 1.5R | 76.3% | 3.51 | 3,353 | 40% |
| 2R | 70.9% | 3.77 | 4,515 | 33% |

Net rises monotonically to the grid edge (2R) — the true peak is at or
beyond it.

- Lit hypothesis 1 (0.5R forfeits the arithmetic edge) CONFIRMED: PF 0.89.
- Lit prior "WR decays fast beyond 1.25R → target 1–1.25R" **REJECTED for
  this trigger**: WR falls only 79→71% from 1R to 2R because the
  footprint trigger's expansion moves run far. 2R is empirically optimal
  and the curve may still be rising past the grid edge (2.5R untested).
- Lit prior "stops 0.75–1.25 ATR" REJECTED in shape: 0.4× the signal stop
  wins. Reconciliation: the trigger's stop is *signal-derived* (break of
  trigger structure), not ATR-scaled — at 0.4× it is not a noise-scaled
  distance but a conviction statement. The ATR prior compares different
  things.
- Lit "30–60 min horizon" CONFIRMED (60-bar time exit optimal).

## Open questions (not blocking)

Superseded by the 2026-10-05 section below (extended grid + walk-forward):
2.5–3R now tested, walk-forward done. The only remaining gate is
real-fill verification of the 0.5pt round-trip assumption.

# Extended grid + walk-forward (2026-10-05) — SUPERSEDES THE PICK

Grid extended per the open questions: stops 0.25–0.6, targets to 3R,
sizes to ×4 (225 combos × 5 sizes). Then rolling walk-forward
(150-train → 30-test, 16 windows) as the multiple-comparisons guardrail.

## Extended plateau (train, constrained)

Top-60 passing rows: PF 3.29–3.66, all inside **s0.3–0.4 × t1.75–3.0 ×
x45–75 × 3–4**. Densest cells: stop 0.35 (14/30), target 2.0–2.5, time
60, size 3.5. The old winner (s0.4/t2/x60/×3, $467,738 train) sits
MID-PACK now — the plateau moved, and it moved toward 2.25–2.5R targets.

Grid-search bias, caught live: the #1 train pick (s0.35/t2/x45/**×4**)
**breaches the test window** (2026-09-11). Unconstrained "biggest size
wins train" is not safe out-of-sample — the walk-forward confirms below.

## WR decay extended past 2R (s0.35 / x60 / 0.5pt)

| Target | WR | PF | net pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2R | 72.2% | 3.83 | 3,967 |
| 2.25R | 69.2% | 3.82 | 4,372 |
| 2.5R | 66.1% | 3.69 | 4,641 |
| 3R | 60.4% | 3.53 | **5,119** |

Net points keep rising to 3R — the curve has no cliff, confirming the
trigger's expansion moves run far. PF peaks at 2R (3.83) and holds ≥3.53
through 3R. 2.25R is the PF-peak/robustness sweet spot.

## New pick

**Stop 0.35× · target 2.25R · 60-bar exit · ×3.5** (plateau center;
t2.5/x75 and t2/x60 are plateau-equal neighbors).

- Full history (649 sessions): WR 69.2% · PF 3.82 · 4,372 pts ·
  **$844,418 @ ×3.5 · dd −$1,794 · eval PASS** (old winner: $720,413).
- Year stability: 2024 PF 3.39/$230,612 · 2025 PF 3.58/$301,850 ·
  2026 PF 4.54/$307,280 — all three PASS.
- More cost-robust than the old winner: ×3 survives 0.75pt (old ×3
  breached there), ×2 survives 1.0pt. ×3.5 still needs ≈0.5pt.

## Walk-forward (150-train → 30-test, 16 windows)

- **14/16 windows PASS**; 2 local breaches, both sized ×3–×4.
- **10/16 windows independently re-select the same plateau**
  (s0.35 with t2.25–2.5, mostly x45–60) — the pick is not a
  train-window artifact; the data keeps converging to the same region.
- Aggregate WF $729k vs static winner $571k on identical segments, but
  the WF picks ×4 in 10 windows and that is exactly where its 2 local
  breaches live. **×4 is past the safe envelope; ×3–×3.5 is the max
  that never breaches at 0.5pt.**

## Cost ladder (per-config size, all years)

Same shape as before — strategy-level ceiling, not config-level:
at 1.0pt every scaled config breaches; the base ×1 config is the only
survivor at ≥1.5pt. The actionable envelope:

| real round-trip | max size (new pick) |
|---|---|
| 0.5pt | ×3.5 ($844k, dd −$1,794) |
| 0.6–0.75pt | ×3 ($621k @ 0.75pt, PASS) |
| **0.95pt (measured live)** | **×2 ($360k, PASS) — ×3 breaches** |
| 1.0pt | ×2 ($346k, PASS) |

Live measurement (TRADE_REVIEW_2026-10-02): fills FIFO gross +$430 vs
net +$61.40 across 388 sides ⇒ **≈$0.95/side ≈ 0.95pt round trip** on
MNQ. Fee-schedule floor would be ≈$0.73/side (0.73pt). The 0.5pt
convention the backtests used is optimistic by ~2×; at measured cost
**×2 is the honest live size** — ×3/×3.5 require costs ≤0.75pt.
Signal→fill entry drift on losers (median ~2pts adverse, review finding
#4) sits ON TOP of this and is not modeled by the cost parameter — the
bracket-anchoring fix (absolute stopLoss/takeProfit at signal prices,
review finding #1) is the lever that claws part of it back.

## 3R variant (2026-10-05, closing the last question)

s0.35/t3/x60 vs the 2.25R winner:

- Verdict: **the pick stands** (s0.35/t2.25/x60, ×2 at measured cost).
  A 3R variant is only interesting if live costs get ≤0.75pt.

## Remaining gate (live, not backtest)

- Real-fill verification is settled: measured ≈0.95pt round trip ⇒ ×2.

  signal prices) + resolving the $0.73 vs $0.95 fee discrepancy.

# Sizing cap — deriving the max realistic micro cap (2026-10-02)

Question: instead of an arbitrary "max 15 micros," what is the MAX realistic
contract cap that doesn't allow ridiculously small stop losses?

Method: combined momentum + expansion stream (MOM_PROD/EXP_PROD), sequential
one-position-at-a-time, first-touch, 0.5 pt cost, $0.95/side commissions,
649 sessions. Runner: `scripts/sizingCapStudy.ts`.

## The cap ⇔ implied minimum stop

Under cap C with the fixed $170 budget, the smallest stop that still deploys
the full budget is **170 ÷ (2C)** points:

| Cap | Full budget only for stops ≥ |
|---|---|
| 30 (status quo) | 2.83 pts — below the 3-pt floor, cap never binds |
| 21 | 4.05 pts |
| 17 | 5.0 pts |
| 15 | 5.67 pts |

So the cap is a *soft minimum-stop enforcement*: it cannot remove a small
stop, but it stops small stops from getting full size.

## Where the edge lives by stop width

| Stop | Share of trades | WR | PF | expR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3–4 pts | **38.3%** | 74.0% | **2.11** | **0.33** |
| 4–5 pts | 22.8% | 77.6% | 2.78 | 0.44 |
| 5–6 pts | 13.9% | 79.5% | 3.21 | 0.50 |
| 6–7 pts | 9.3% | 81.2% | 3.70 | 0.55 |
| 7–8 pts | 5.1% | 83.2% | 4.32 | 0.60 |

The 3–4 pt bucket is the "ridiculous" zone: the largest bucket (38% of
trades) with the weakest edge by a wide margin — and under flat $170 sizing
those weakest trades got the SAME dollars as the best. The edge steps up
sharply at the 4-pt boundary (PF 2.11 → 2.78).

## Cap sweep (live tiers on)

| Cap | Total | Worst day | >$900d | $/vol | Trades at cap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | +$166.2k | −$1,129 | 11 | 435 | 0% |
| 24 | +$166.1k | −$1,078 | 9 | 441 | 19% |
| 20 | +$164.7k | −$1,023 | 8 | 458 | 35% |
| **15** | +$157.0k | −$902 | 3 | 486 | 54% |
| 12 | +$143.5k | −$813 | 0 | **496** | 66% |
| 10 | +$130.2k | −$853 | 0 | 491 | 75% |

Every cap reduction below 30 improves the worst day and $/vol; the $/vol
sweet spot is 12–15. Cap 15 costs 5.5% of total for a 20% better worst day.

## Min-risk floor sweep — the sharper lever

| minRisk | Trades | Total | Worst day | >$900d | $/vol |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 (status quo) | 5,556 | +$166.2k | −$1,129 | 11 | 435 |
| **4** | 3,427 | +$156.1k (−6%) | **−$743** | 3 | **510** |
| 5 | 2,158 | +$120.3k (−28%) | −$829 | 1 | 432 |
| 6 | 1,383 | +$86.2k (−48%) | −$850 | 0 | 350 |

Dropping ONLY the 3–4 pt bucket (minRisk 4) costs 6% of total while cutting
the worst day 34% and raising $/vol 435 → 510 — strictly better than any cap
on every risk metric. At minRisk 4 the budget implies 21 contracts exactly,
so cap 21 never binds — it becomes a pure backstop.

## Final design — the widen floor at 3.5 pts (adopted)

The contract cap stayed at the plan's 30 micros and the max-stop ceiling was
left alone (big stops stay). The one change: **structural stops tighter than
3.5 pts widen to entry ∓ 3.5** (`riskFloorPts: 3.5` on MOM_PROD/EXP_PROD);
the 1R target follows. Stops under minRiskPts (3) still never trade — the
hard floor is checked BEFORE the widen, because rescuing the sub-3 zone was
measured to cost 39% of total and to produce −$2.7k days.

### The floor sweep (where does the return peak?)

| Floor | Trades | Total | Worst day | >$900d | $/vol |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| off (structural) | 5,556 | +$166.2k | −$1,129 | 11 | 435 |
| 3.25 | 5,553 | +$167.4k | −$1,114 | 11 | 436 |
| **3.5** | **5,550** | **+$169.4k** | −$1,074 | 9 | 448 |
| 3.75 | 5,543 | +$168.6k | −$1,047 | 9 | 450 |
| 4 | 5,532 | +$167.8k | −$1,040 | 8 | 446 |
| 4.25 | 5,518 | +$161.2k | −$1,366 | 10 | 415 |
| 4.5 | 5,511 | +$158.4k | −$1,280 | 10 | 407 |
| 5 | 5,486 | +$158.0k | −$1,634 | 10 | 404 |
| 6 | 5,394 | +$150.0k | −$1,541 | 10 | 376 |
| 8 | 5,151 | +$118.0k | −$1,376 | 6 | 302 |

Return peaks at **3.5** (+1.9% vs structural, worst day −5%); the minimum
floor capturing the peak is 3.5. Floors past ~4 are strictly dominated —
less total AND worse worst days (4.25–5.5 produce the table's worst tails,
−$1,366 to −$1,634). The original 4 was an eyeballed integer bucket edge;
the sweep refined it to 3.5.

Contracts: with stops ≥ 3.5 pts, $170 budget ⇒ up to 24 contracts, so the
30-micro cap never binds — the stop floor, not a contract cap, is what
bounds size.

# Vol/structure SIZING study — stop × size knobs, zero vetoes (2026-10-04)

**Question:** never gate trades — instead sweep how STOP SIZE and CONTRACT
SIZE respond to the macro regime (realized vol, VIX, daily/weekly swing
structure). Do any of the knobs beat the baseline?

**Method:** `web/scripts/volSizingStudy.ts` — 649-session R2 replay of the
prod momentum detectors (flush + expansion), lookahead-free regime features
(prior-session realized vol percentile; prior-day VIX close from the CBOE
1990+ CSV joined strictly before the session; HH/HL/LH/LL/CHOP structure
from prior sessions via `lib/htfStructure`). Scoring = house rules: 0.5 pt
cost, 60-bar time exit, first-touch pessimistic, one-trade-at-a-time
sequential. Stop variants re-score the 1R box (stop × mult, target = 1R of
the new stop); size variants scale pnlPts (a sizeMult fill under the fixed
$170 risk budget — the `htfRegimeStudy` convention). Account impact via the
MFF Rapid EOD 50k sim. Baseline: **n=2,326 · WR 76.4% · PF 2.86 · 5,456 pts ·
$160,711 · maxDD −$1,379 · funded[test] $53,049**.

## Results

### A · Uniform grid (stopMult × sizeMult) — net pts / PF

| stop | ×0.5 | ×0.75 | ×1.0 | ×1.25 | ×1.5 | ×2.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| s0.75 | 2.3k/3.53 | 3.4k/3.53 | 4.6k/3.53 | 5.7k/3.53 | 6.9k/3.53 | 9.2k/3.53 |
| s1.0 | 2.7k/2.86 | 4.1k/2.86 | 5.5k/2.86 | 6.8k/2.86 | 8.2k/2.86 | 10.9k/2.86 |
| s1.25 | 2.7k/2.22 | 4.1k/2.22 | 5.4k/2.22 | 6.8k/2.22 | 8.2k/2.22 | 10.9k/2.22 |
| s1.5 | 2.8k/1.95 | 4.2k/1.95 | 5.6k/1.95 | 7.0k/1.95 | 8.4k/1.95 | 11.2k/1.95 |

### B–D · conditional variants (no veto)

| Variant | PF | $ net | maxDD | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base s1.0 ×1.0 | 2.86 | $160,711 | −$1,379 | — |
| **s0.75 ×1.0** | **3.53** | **$178,237** | **−$898** | **winner** |
| s1.25 / s1.5 | 2.22 / 1.95 | $128,795 / $110,582 | worse | wider stops lose monotonically |
| stop×1.25 in HIGH vol | 2.55 | $149,740 | −$1,379 | beats uniform s1.25, still loses to base |
| size by vol (L1.25/M1/H0.75) | 2.82 | $154,925 | −$1,723 | no |
| both vol (stop+size) | 2.58 | $146,696 | −$1,723 | no |
| size by daily structure | 2.80 | $153,760 | −$1,723 | no |
| size by daily+weekly structure | 2.82 | $174,663 | −$2,068 | **eval BREACH 2024-05-22** — no |
| stop×1.25 in HIGH vix | 2.62 | $152,517 | −$1,379 | no |
| size by vix (L1.25/M1/H0.75) | 2.85 | $166,280 | −$1,723 | +3.5% net, worse DD — marginal no |
| both vix (stop+size) | 2.67 | $160,133 | −$1,723 | no |

### Why the conditional knobs failed — the regime buckets are flat or inverted

Base trades by regime (PF / net pts): realized-vol terciles **2.65 / 2.76 /
3.06** — the HIGH-vol bucket is the BEST cell (953 trades, 2,668 pts = half
the total). VIX terciles: 2.81 / 2.82 / 3.13. Daily structure: agree 2.70 /
**counter 3.13** / neutral 2.87. Weekly: agree 2.73 / counter 2.78 / neutral
3.31.

So "vol targeting" (cut size in high vol) was backwards for THIS trigger:
high-vol sessions produce the huge bars the strategy feeds on. And
"structure agreement" up-weighted the WORSE bucket (counter-trend trades are
the better cell — consistent with `htf-short-pullback-2026-10-02.md`).

## Extension run 2 — COT + Treasury curve added (2026-10-04)

Historical data now wired in, all PIT-joined: **COT** (CFTC Socrata, 250
weekly reports, noncomm = spec, publish = report_date+3d) and the **daily
Treasury par curve** (home.treasury.gov CSVs 2023–2026 → 2s10s / 10y−3m / 10y
level + 3m change).

### New conditional variants (no veto)

| Variant | PF | $ net | maxDD | funded[test] |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **size×1.25 when 2s10s positive** | 2.88 | **$192,859** | −$1,504 | **$66,312** |
| size×1.25 when positioning RISING | 2.87 | $181,594 | −$1,438 | $58,875 |
| size×1.25 when positioning FALLING | 2.86 | $180,008 | −$1,664 | $60,486 |
| size×0.75 when COT crowded (≥90th pct) | 2.88 | $152,830 | −$1,379 | $52,689 |
| stop×1.25 when 2s10s inverted | 2.71 | $154,990 | −$1,203 | $53,049 |
| crowd+rates combo | 2.73 | $147,619 | −$902 | $52,689 |
| (recap) base s1.0 | 2.86 | $160,711 | −$1,379 | $53,049 |
| (recap) s0.75 | **3.53** | $178,237 | **−$898** | $53,510 |

### New regime buckets (base trades)

- **COT percentile:** 0–33 pct PF 2.94 · **33–66 pct PF 3.46 (best)** ·
  66–100 pct PF 2.54 (crowded = worst, still profitable).
- **COT side:** net-long era (most of the window) 2.77 · net-short 3.21.
- **2s10s:** inverted PF 2.53 (489 sessions) vs positive PF 2.94 (1,837) —
  the curve regime genuinely separates the tape; the inversion era was the
  worse half.
- **10y 3m change:** rising-yield era 3.17 vs falling 2.84.

### Honest read

The 2s10s and COT-shift "winners" are mostly *size-up-in-the-better-bucket*
effects — both condition on ~half-to-79% of sessions, so they partly
recapitulate "just size up overall" (the strategy has positive expectancy in
every bucket; any large ×1.25 subset raises $ net while growing drawdown).
The one cleanly interpretable macro result is the **2s10s bucket split**
(inverted = worse tape) and the **COT middle-vs-crowded** ordering. None of
the conditional knobs beat s0.75 on risk-adjusted terms (maxDD). Next steps:
train/test the 2s10s split, and a finer stop grid (0.5–0.9) to confirm the
s0.75 plateau.

## Verdict

1. **Tighter stops win** — s0.75: PF 2.86→3.53, WR 76.4→80.7%, $ net +11%,
   maxDD −35%. Mechanism: the fixed $170 risk budget buys more contracts at
   a 25%-tighter stop AND the edge lives in quick 1R hits, not tail
   outcomes. Needs the plateau discipline: sweep 0.6/0.7/0.8/0.9 next.
2. **Macro-conditional sizing does not pay here** (vol/vix/structure all
   neutral-to-negative after drawdown), for a measurable reason: the
   trigger is regime-robust and the "scary" cells are the good ones.
3. Next experiments: finer stop grid around 0.75 (incl. 0.5), target
   multiples (0.75R/1R/1.25R) × the winner, the same grid on the RTH soft
   strategy, and a train/test split of the winning knob.
kelly-mode:
# Kelly mode — backtest sizer + self-updating live chip (2026-10-07)

**Idea source:** Medallion documentary analysis
(`docs/research/medallion-documentary-2026-10-07.md`) and the experiment
list (`docs/research/medallion-ideas-2026-10-07.md`, idea #2 — "size to
the measured edge").

**Status:** SHIPPED as code, **journal-only in live mode**. `KELLY_MODE`
and `KELLY_LIVE_USE` are both OFF — no Coolify env has been changed and
none may be without the rule-4 approval. Live sizing today is byte-for-
byte the flat $100 day plan.

---

## 1. What it is

One estimator, two consumers (the "one book" principle):

- **`web/lib/kelly.ts`** — pure, client-safe Kelly math:
  `f* = p − (1−p)/b`, with `b = avg win R ÷ avg loss R` from realized
  trades. Estimates are **shrunk toward a prior** (beta-style pull on
  the win rate, R-means pulled toward the prior too), so a thin sample
  can never flip sizing on one lucky streak.
- **Backtests:** `dollarizeKelly()` walks a dated trade sequence forward
  and sizes every trade from **prior trades only** (per-family state, no
  lookahead; per-family config resolvers supported), returning the same
  `DollarizedTrade[]` shape that `simulateAccount()` consumes — the MFF
  sim is untouched.
- **Live cards:** `kellyLiveChip()` (`web/lib/kellyLive.ts`) folds the
  last `KELLY_WINDOW` decided outcomes of a family from the `signals`
  table into the same estimator and returns a chip. Best-effort — any DB
  hiccup → null → flat plan.
- **Live-guard replay:** `web/lib/guardReplay.ts` — the day-plan guard
  stack (daily floor, profit arm, give-back, consistency-day halt,
  floor-margin halt, target halt, dd600→half sizing) replayed trade by
  trade, mirroring `accountGuard.ts` guardCheck 1:1 and reading the SAME
  env knobs. `simulateAccountGuarded()` (lib/propAccount.ts) composes it
  with the MFF sim, and `BT_GUARD=1` switches the offline sweep runner
  (`db/backtest.ts` → `lib/backtest.ts`) to the guarded path — backtests
  and the live executor now enforce the same stack.

## 2. The sizing mode (relative Kelly)

The flat $100 is the anchor. `risk$ = flatRisk × kellyMult × f / fRef`,
where `fRef` is the **prior's** own Kelly fraction:

- thin live evidence → estimate = prior → risk = flat exactly;
- winning run → risk climbs toward `KELLY_MAX_RISK` (150);
- losing run → risk shrinks toward `KELLY_MIN_RISK` (25);
- edge gone (`f ≤ 0`) → **stand aside** (0 contracts, 0 pnl) — Kelly
  doctrine: no edge, no bet.

Why relative and not absolute: absolute Kelly on the $2,000 MLL buffer
at the measured 77.5% edge says "risk $550/trade" — full Kelly is
insane on a prop account. The day plan's $100 is already ~0.09× Kelly;
the relative mode keeps that conservatism and only moves sizing when
the *measured* edge moves. The ratio of Kelly fractions is exactly the
ratio of optimal bet sizes at the two edge estimates.

**Known wrinkle (found by the validation, §5):** when a family's prior
edge is *marginal*, `fRef` is tiny and the ratio `f/fRef` is unstable —
early wins blow it up and full-Kelly over-bets. On such families only
half-Kelly (`KELLY_MULT=0.5`) is safe. This is exactly why the sizing
switch stays OFF: the knob discipline has to be per-family, and that
decision is a rule-4 one, not a code one.

## 3. Env knobs (all default OFF)

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `KELLY_MODE` | unset | `1` computes the self-updating chip on momentum + RTH cards (journal only) |
| `KELLY_LIVE_USE` | unset | `1` switches card sizing to the Kelly risk — **rule-4 approval required, never enabled** |
| `KELLY_WINDOW` | 60 | live trades examined per family |
| `KELLY_MULT` | 1 | fraction of the Kelly ratio (0.5 = half) |
| `KELLY_MAX_RISK` | 150 | $ ceiling per trade |
| `KELLY_MIN_RISK` | 25 | $ floor (stand-aside overrides it) |
| `KELLY_MAX_FRAC` | 0.5 | cap on f* itself — a shrunk estimate is never trusted past 50% |

All seven are registered in the daybook `SETTINGS_KEYS` snapshot, so any
variation's knobs stay reproducible.

## 4. Live behavior (what actually changed)

- `KELLY_MODE=1`: the momentum and RTH cards print a chip —
  `KELLY 41t 79% → $112 (journal) · ` — and store `{n, p, b, f, fRef,
  ratio, risk, skip, family, window, priorWr}` in `signals.features`.
  The chip **self-updates**: every card's chip reflects every decided
  trade in the signals table up to that moment (the outcome scorer
  writes win/loss/time as bars print). Sizing stays flat.
- `KELLY_LIVE_USE=1` **and** `KELLY_MODE=1`: the card's risk budget
  becomes the Kelly risk (still through `applyDayTier`, so day tiers and
  the dd600→half rule still apply on top). Stand-aside chips never size
  a card.
- Everything is best-effort and wrapped: a Kelly failure can never block
  or change a card beyond the flat plan.
- RTH cards now also record `family: "rth"` in features (was only on
  veto records) — the chip query filters on it.

## 5. Validation — grounded in the live rule stack

- **Unit tests:** `web/tests/kelly.test.ts` (12: the documentary's
  50.75% → 1.5% edge, shrinkage, stand-aside, R-multiple folding, caps
  and floors, no-lookahead, per-family independence) and
  `web/tests/guardReplay.test.ts` (12: pins every guard rule — daily
  floor, the documented one-more-trade arm, give-back, consistency-day,
  floor-margin, target halt, dd hysteresis, stand-asides, per-day reset,
  drawdown diagnostics, env-knob mirror). Full suite green (651 pass) +
  `tsc --noEmit` clean.
- **Backtest study:** `web/scripts/kellySizingStudy.ts` — 652 sessions,
  run through `guardReplay` (the same module the guarded sweeps use).

### 5.1 What the study replays (the rules coverage)

| Layer | Modeled | Where |
|---|---|---|
| EOD trailing MLL $2,000 | ✓ | `simulateAccount` (floor trails at closes, never down) |
| Funded floor lock at $100 | ✓ | `simulateAccount` |
| Eval $3,000 target + 4 min days + 30% consistency | ✓ | `simulateAccount` + guard consistency-day halt |
| Payout buffer $2,100 + $500 steps | ✓ | `simulateAccount` funded |
| 30-micro contract cap, min 1, floor($ ÷ $2/pt) | ✓ | `momentumSize` |
| Kelly caps ($150/$25/0.5 frac) | ✓ | `kellyEstimate` |
| DAILY_LOSS_FLOOR 250 | ✓ | `guardReplay` (halt new entries) |
| PROFIT_ARM 400 one-more-trade | ✓ | `guardReplay` (the documented rule: first LOSS after arming ends the day — same as apPlan's runDay) |
| Give-back protection 0.5 × dayPeak, $250 floor | ✓ | `guardReplay` |
| Consistency-day halt at $900 | ✓ | `guardReplay` (eval) |
| GUARD_MARGIN 500 floor halt | ✓ | `guardReplay` |
| dd600→half sizing, 300 hysteresis | ✓ | `guardReplay` (contracts × 0.5) |
| Live replay semantics: every detector signal, 0.95 pt cost, −1.75 pt drift on losers | ✓ | study replay (gapOnlyValidation conventions) |
| RTH live limit bracket (0.5× stop, 2.5R, limit fill) | ✓ | separate section (rthLimitValidation model) |
| All families interleaved (the pool the day plan actually trades) | ✓ | POOL section, per-family Kelly books |
| **News blackouts** | ✗ | not in the archive — documented gap |
| **Operator overrides / ticket veto** | ✗ | live-only decisions |
| **EXP retrace-arm limit fill** | ✗ | market entry used for EXP; retrace arm is a separate harness |
| **Open family** | ✗ | separate $170 budget — see PLAYBOOK |
| **Size tiers** | ✗ | OFF live (SIZE_TIERS unset) — matched |
| **10,000 day-orderings Monte Carlo** | ✗ | apPlanSweep's blow-rate protocol; this study is chronological + both stages |

### 5.2 Results — 652 sessions, full guard stack + drawdowns

`node --import ../scripts/ts-loader.mjs scripts/kellySizingStudy.ts --offline`
(cost 0.95 pt · drift −1.75 pt losers · priors from train ≤ 2025-12-31).

**POOL (MOM + EXP + RTH interleaved — the actual day plan):**

| Config | Eval | worst day | max DD | mean risk | stand-asides | halts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| flat $100 | PASS day 16 | −$407 | $768 | $94 | — | floor 4 · gb 3 · cons 1 |
| kelly m1 cap150 | PASS day 18 | **−$347** | **$642** | $96 | 0 | floor 3 · arm 2 · gb 1 · cons 1 |
| kelly m1 cap100 | no-pass · $3,025 (bar $3,047 — $22 short) | −$347 | $642 | $90 | 0 | floor 3 · arm 2 · gb 1 · cons 1 |
| kelly m0.5 cap100 | PASS day 27 | **−$273** | **$403** | $44 | 0 | floor 2 |

**RTH market 0.75R:** flat PASS day 15 ($3,027); kelly m1 cap150 PASS
day 22 ($3,016, maxDD $570 vs flat $880).

**RTH live limit bracket (marginal edge, fRef ≈ 0.02):** flat bleeds to
−$857 with 572 margin halts (a genuinely losing cell, not a consistency
issue). Kelly m1 cap150 **over-bets on early luck** (1,223 stand-asides
then 74 trades sized up at the cap → −$1,098). Kelly **m0.5** cap100 is
the only safe cell: 1,223 stand-asides, PASS day 237, maxDD $894 vs
flat's $1,502. This is the finding in §2 — on marginal-edge families
the mult must be 0.5, not 1.

**No config breaches the funded account in any cell.** The guards fire
exactly as live (halts by reason are in every row).

### 5.3 Reading the results

- On strong-edge families (pool, RTH market) Kelly ≈ flat on speed and
  improves the tails: pool worst-day −15%, maxDD −16% (m1) and
  −33% / −48% (m0.5, at the cost of a slower eval: day 27 vs 16).
- **The 30% consistency rule is SOFT — a big day never fails the eval.**
  It raises the effective target to `max($3,000, bestDay ÷ 0.3)`. The
  pool m1 cap100 cell looks like a failure in the table but is not one:
  its best day ($914 — a one-trade overshoot past the $900/day halt,
  which is an entry gate) raised the bar to $3,047, and the
  chronological path ended at $3,025 — **$22 short of the raised bar,
  with the highest equity of the three configs**. Live, the account
  simply keeps trading toward $3,047. The `accountLine` no-pass line
  now prints `needs $3,047 (30% bar raised by best day $914)` so this
  can't be misread as a hard fail. The $900/day halt itself is OUR
  day-plan rule (it keeps the bar pinned at $3,000), not an MFF
  failure.
- On marginal-edge families, full relative Kelly is dangerous and
  half-Kelly is the floor. **The mode is only as safe as its per-family
  mult.**
- **Verdict:** safe and useful as a journal-only self-updating edge
  book. The sizing switch stays OFF until a funded-stage decision under
  rule 4, and then only as: mult 0.5, cap $100, per-family prior — the
  conservative cell — with a fresh run of this study + the ap-plan
  10k-ordering sweep on top.

### 5.4 Using the live-guard backtest everywhere

- Any study script: `simulateAccountGuarded(rows, stage)` from
  `lib/propAccount` returns `{ sim, guard }` — the MFF sim on top of the
  guard-stack replay (halts, drawdowns, stand-asides included).
- The offline threshold sweeps: `BT_GUARD=1 node --import
  ../scripts/ts-loader.mjs db/backtest.ts` writes guarded eval/funded
  account sections + guard diagnostics into the results JSON.
- The guard replay reads the SAME env knobs as the live guard
  (`DAILY_LOSS_FLOOR`, `PROFIT_ARM`, `GUARD_GIVEBACK_*`, `DD_HALF_*`,
  `MFF_GUARD_MARGIN`, `MFF_CONSISTENCY_CAP`, …) via
  `guardConfigFromEnv()`, so a backtest run with the live env follows
  the live configuration exactly.

## 6. Caveats

- The study replays the RTH live-limit bracket with TTL 5 and
  one-position-at-a-time (a conservative variant — the official
  rthLimitValidation reports PF 1.49 on 9,009 trades with looser
  semantics); its job here is sizing behavior on a marginal-edge
  family, not a re-validation of the bracket.
- News blackouts, overrides and the EXP retrace-arm fill are not in the
  archive harness (documented, not silent).
- Zero-pnl trades (flat/time exits) carry no R information and never
  touch the state, by design.
- The live chip uses playbook priors as anchors; backtests derive priors
  from the train window only — no lookahead.

# Daily give-back protection — analysis + replay study (2026-10-02)

## Today's fluctuation, decomposed

Session realized P&L: **peak +$642.8 at 13:44:45 → trough +$205.0 at 14:25:11
(−$437.8 give-back, 68% of the peak)** → closed +$250.4.

The give-back was three events in the 14:15–14:25 window:

1. **14:15 long −$98** — RTH long filled and stopped in 6 seconds into a falling
   afternoon tape (legitimate loss, but the tape had turned).
2. **14:19 long −$180** — stopped at 31021.5 (legitimate loss).
3. **14:21 stacked double-entry −$180 (bug)** — the verified re-send re-entered
   the SAME 14:19 card 105s later because its broker verification read
   "no working order, no position" (a stale/empty CrossTrade read) even though
   the original order had been ACCEPTED ("REST placed" at 14:20:11). Two 9-lots
   held the same signal; both stopped at 31021.5. The re-send feature was
   scoped too wide: it re-sent after SUCCESSFUL sends with no visible fill
   (a data-lag), not only after FAILED sends.

**Fix shipped**: the verified re-send now applies ONLY when the original place
attempt returned not-ok (`sendFailed`). A successful send with no visible fill
alerts ("SEND OK BUT NO FILL VISIBLE — do NOT re-send") and never re-enters.
Regression tests: `resendDecision` + the 14:21 stack scenario.

## Replay study — do protection rules pay? (648 sessions, Globex momentum, live sizing)

| Rule | Total profit | vs baseline | Worst day | Days halted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | $60,316 | 100% | −$742 | — |
| give-back 30%/≥$150 | $45,627 | 76% | **−$249** | 330 |
| give-back 40%/≥$200 | $47,401 | 79% | −$449 | 299 |
| **give-back 50%/≥$250** | **$54,486** | **90%** | **−$496** | **105** |
| daily loss limit −$300 | $54,048 | 90% | −$523 | 74 |
| stop after 2 losses | $56,270 | 93% | −$496 | 72 |
| stop after 3 losses | $59,971 | 99% | −$741 | 12 |

Readings:

- **Consecutive-loss rules are nearly useless here** (99% of profit, no
  protection) — consistent with the research (a stop rule should not pretend
  the third loss predicts the fourth; [Trader's Second Brain: When to Stop
  Trading After Losses](https://traderssecondbrain.com/guides/when-to-stop-trading-after-losses)).
- **Give-back protection is a smoothing trade, not a free lunch**: it costs
  10–24% of total profit to cut the worst day by 33–66%. The 50%/$250 variant
  is the chosen balance: 90% of the edge, worst day −$496, halts only 105 of
  660 days.
- **Honest caveat**: today's give-back came mostly from OPEN positions stopping
  out — the rule halts NEW entries, so it would not have recovered the $437;
  it prevents the NEXT entries from deepening a bad day. The double-entry bug
  fix ($180) is the part of today that was recoverable — and is recovered.
- Further reading: [SMB — A Rule for Giving Back Profits](https://www.smbtraining.com/blog/a-4-the-trading-community-a-rule-for-giving-back-profits),
  [FTMO — risk management in practice](https://ftmo.com/en/blog/risk-management-and-psychology-in-practice-how-to-trade-without-stress/).

## Tiered sizing — smaller bets as the day's profit climbs

Replay (648 sessions, live sizing): tiered contracts by day P&L:

| Schedule | Total | vs base | >$900 breach days | Tiered trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline (full size all day) | $60,316 | 100% | **4** | — |
| **2/3 @ +$300, 1/3 @ +$600** | **$58,573** | **97%** | **0** | 226 |
| 1/2 @ +$250, 1/4 @ +$500 | $56,849 | 94% | 0 | 309 |

The default schedule (2/3 @ $300, 1/3 @ $600) keeps 97% of total profit and
eliminates the days that would breach the $900 consistency cap — the cap makes
the day's payoff curve concave, so shrinking above +$300 costs almost nothing
while removing the eval-failing tail. This is cheaper than the give-back halt
(which costs 10-24%) because it fires on GREEN days, where the marginal dollar
has negative expected value anyway. `SIZE_TIERS` env overrides; `SIZE_TIERS=""`
disables.

## Integrated full-stack backtest (scripts/riskStackStudy.ts, 648 sessions)

All four live families (momentum rr1.0 + expansion + RTH + open drive),
globally sequenced one-position-at-a-time, ladder exits, LIVE sizing
($170-budget momentum, $200-capped fixed-9 RTH/open), commissions, then
the protection layers toggled, through the MFF account simulator:

| Variant | Trades | Total | Median day | Worst day | >$900 days | Sim |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fixed 1R, no protections | 16,841 | +$640k | +$963 | −$1,387 | 342 | PASS |
| **ladder, no protections** | 15,745 | +$2.9M | +$4,160 | −$2,597 | 600 | **BREACH 2026-08-05** |
| ladder + day tiers | 15,745 | +$1.34M | +$2,004 | −$1,702 | 599 | PASS |
| ladder + give-back halt | 9,041 | +$1.70M | +$872 | −$1,128 | 322 | PASS |
| **full live stack** | 11,846 | +$1.0M | +$1,627 | −$1,128 | 434 | **PASS** |

Headline findings:

1. **The raw ladder breaches the account** — without protections it hits the
   trailing drawdown in Aug 2026 of the sim. The protection layers are what
   make the ladder survivable: every protected variant passes.
2. **Tiers are the cheapest protection** (ladder → +tiers keeps 46% of the raw
   total while turning BREACH into PASS); the give-back halt costs more total
   but produces the shallowest worst day (−$1,128) and the fewest big days.
3. **The full stack passes with the best risk profile**: worst day −$1,128 vs
   −$2,597 raw, and the eval completes.
4. Caveats: totals are optimistic vs live (no news gaps, 0.5-pt execution cost,
   every RTH signal taken, no execution misses) — read the RATIOS, not the
   absolute dollars. And note the "$900 breach days" column is our own
   conservative day-halt interpretation; MFF's actual rule is best-day ≤ 30%
   of end-of-eval total profit, which the simulator enforces in its
   consist ✓ flag.

## Implemented

- `accountGuard`: `dayPeak` tracked + persisted to Neon; new `halt-giveback`
  verdict — no new entries once the day gives back more than
  `max(GUARD_GIVEBACK_FLOOR, GUARD_GIVEBACK_PCT × dayPeak)` (defaults $250 /
  50%; env `GUARD_GIVEBACK_PCT=0` disables). Resets on the calendar rollover.
- `execWatch`: verified re-send scoped to failed sends only (see above).
- Tests: give-back trigger/floor/disable/rollover + resendDecision matrix.

# Retrace slippage sensitivity — 2026-10-04

**Question:** does the expansion-retrace edge survive entry slippage, or must the
entry fill at the limit price? (Motivation: the 2026-10-04 reopen — the live
market-order path filled 14.75 pts past the tape fill and the OCO closed it
instantly; decision needed between "always broker limits" vs "keep market +
block on drift".)

**Method** (`web/scripts/retraceSlippageStudy.ts`): replay the expansion retrace
over the 649-session R2 archive with the exact machinery of
`entryQualityStudy.ts`'s "exp retrace" cell — 5 bars, 1 pt behind the signal
close, fill at the limit-or-better (gap-through), brackets anchored at the
fill, ladder exits (0.5-pt round-trip cost inside the scorer), live sizing /
day tiers / give-back halt — then sweep an ADVERSE offset on top of the fill.
`0.0 pts` = a resting broker limit at the retrace level, i.e. the backtest's
own model and the faithful execution.

## Results (649 sessions, split 2026-01-01)

| offset (adverse pts) | n | W/L | WR% | net | PF | $/trade | medDay | worstDay |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0.0 (limit)** | 2346 | 1470/876 | 62.7% | **+$18,809** | 1.05 | +$8 | +$136 | −$3,961 |
| 0.5 | 2368 | 1302/1066 | 55.0% | −$115,905 | 0.77 | −$49 | −$58 | −$4,492 |
| 1.0 | 2358 | 1119/1239 | 47.5% | −$256,475 | 0.59 | −$109 | −$264 | −$5,006 |
| 2.0 | 2368 | 785/1583 | 33.2% | −$565,416 | 0.32 | −$239 | −$574 | −$5,332 |
| 3.0 | 2611 | 513/2098 | 19.6% | −$947,965 | 0.16 | −$363 | −$1,147 | −$8,819 |

Leak vs the limit baseline: 0.5 pts → **−$134,714** and **162 winners flipped to
losers**; 1 pt → −$275,284 (323 flips); 2 pts → −$584,224 (603 flips); 3 pts →
−$966,774 (924 flips). Zero flips in the favorable direction — the offset is
pure adverse leakage.

Out-of-sample (TEST ≥ 2026-01-01): 0.0 pts **+$23,211** (66.2% WR) vs 0.5 pts
−$2,059 (60.3% WR) vs 1.0 pts −$41,989 (52.3% WR). The limit fill holds; the
slip does not, in either split.

## Verdict

- The retrace edge is **priced at the limit and dies at half a point of
  slip**. Even 0.5 pt of adverse entry slip flips the strategy from +$18.8K /
  PF 1.05 to −$115.9K / PF 0.77. The live market-order path has therefore been
  leaking the entire edge on every retrace fill — the exact opposite of the
  backtest's assumption.
- **Block-on-drift is NOT a substitute.** The quote gate only cuts the
  pathological tail (>3 pts ≈ −$948K/yr of modeled damage); the 0.5–1 pt
  "normal" slip (which any market order carries) destroys the edge by itself.
- **Backtests: no problem.** Limits are the faithful execution — the study
  already fills at the limit. The broker resting-limit path
  (`CROSSTRADE_LIMIT_ENTRIES=1`, `lib/crossTrade.ts` +
  `lib/execWatch.ts` limit lifecycle) brings live execution IN LINE with the
  model. The market path was the mismatch.
- Remaining live-vs-backtest gap to watch: tape-touched-but-broker-untouched
  retraces expire unfilled (`limit_expired` in `exec_log`) while the backtest
  counts a fill — live under-fills, conservatively. Partial fills of a
  multi-contract resting limit are unmodeled; verify once live before
  trusting the mode.

## Action taken (2026-10-04)

The retrace limit mode shipped behind `CROSSTRADE_LIMIT_ENTRIES=1` (default
OFF pending the one-lot place+cancel verification). A quote-agreement gate
was built and then removed (2026-10-05): no real-time broker-side price
source exists for a Tradovate account (CrossTrade market data is NT8-only;
free external feeds are delayed), so the divergence protection rests on the
limit entries themselves — a resting limit can never fill above its target.
Given these numbers, enable limit entries once that verification passes.
