# Daybook — the DB-less system journal (2026-10-07)

## Why

The 2026-10-07 post-mortem found the trade journal dead:

- The live dashboard container had no `DATABASE_URL` → `exec_log`, `signals`,
  `guard_state`, `trade_analysis` were memory-only, wiped by the 08:37 ET
  redeploy, and `/api/trades` returned `{ok:false, "no DATABASE_URL"}`.
- Neon was quota-blocked (`Your account or project has exceeded the quota` —
  monthly data-transfer cap exceeded; storage at 412/512 MB and climbing),
  refusing NEW connections, so the nightly ingest/reconcile/analysis steps
  could not run at all.

**Can we keep using the DB?** Storage works — the binding constraint is
EGRESS. The workload shape (nightly re-ingest of a 3-week candle window +
dashboard readthrough queries) will keep blowing the free-tier transfer cap
even after a reset. Neon can stay for the rich analytics (equity curve,
scoreboard, hour matrices) whenever it is reachable — but the journal must
not depend on it.

**The DB-less solution:** the daybook. One append-only JSONL per NY trading
day at `GC_DATA_DIR/daybook/<day>.jsonl`, written by the live dashboard
(persistent Coolify volume at `/app/data`) and archived to Cloudflare R2
(free egress) by the nightly jobs container.

## Record types

| t | writer | content |
|---|--------|---------|
| `boot` | dashboard boot | variation fingerprint: git SHA (`BUILD_SHA` ← Coolify `SOURCE_COMMIT`) + full settings snapshot (every strategy/risk/feed knob, secrets masked to a stable sha256 prefix) → `variationId` |
| `signal` | signalFeed → signalHistory | every card emitted AND every veto/skip with entry/stop/target + features (skips were DB-only before) |
| `exec` | execLog | every order attempt/watch decision (redeploys can no longer destroy the evidence) |
| `guard` | accountGuard.save() | day reference + protection state on meaningful events (rollover/arm/dd) |
| `heal` | live.ts | every tape-gap stall episode closed: episode number, ladder steps, duration |
| `dayend` | scripts/daybookConsolidate.ts (nightly) | the consolidated day summary (trades, W/L, net, heal episodes, cap-skip replay, expRetrace quality) |

## Consolidation (nightly, DB-less)

`scripts/daybookConsolidate.ts` pulls the live JSONL from
`/api/daybook?format=jsonl`, reconstructs every trade from the CrossTrade
fill/order record (order-level via `parentId` + sibling-`ocoId` resolution,
fill-level fallback after the ~17:00 session reset), labels trades with
their signal cards, replays RTH cap skips against the collected tape, and
writes `<day>.summary.json` + the `dayend` record. `r2_sync.py upload`
archives the `daybook/` dir.

## Read path

- `GET /api/daybook` — the variation index (fingerprint per day + summaries).
- `GET /api/trades` — falls back to the daybook summaries whenever the DB is
  absent or unreachable.
- `GET /api/gc?action=health` — `buildId` is now the deployed SHA; `domFeed`
  shows the DOM_V2 frame counters; `liveFeed.heal` shows the ladder state.

## The variation log

Every push to `main` auto-deploys → the new process writes a `boot` record
with its `variationId`. The index (`/api/daybook`) therefore shows, per day:
which variation ran, its exact settings, and its day P&L — the settings
fingerprint makes any knob change visible as a new variation.

## Env knobs

- `DAYBOOK_OFF=1` silences journal writes (set by the test loader).
- `BUILD_SHA` — injected by the Dockerfile from Coolify's `SOURCE_COMMIT`
  build arg (`include_source_commit_in_build=true` on the Coolify app).
- `DASHBOARD_URL` — where the consolidation pulls the live JSONL from
  (default: the sslip dashboard URL).

| Net liquidation | $50,966.60 |
| Realized P&L, this session | **+$61.40** (net) |
| Realized P&L, this week | +$966.60 |
| Position / working orders | flat / none |

Session gross (fills, FIFO): **+$430** ⇒ implied all-in costs ≈ **$0.95/side** across 388 sides
(≈$368 total). Verify this against MFF's current micro fee schedule — at the usual $0.62+$0.11
the costs should be ≈$299, so either fees are higher than assumed or a ~$70 detail needs a second
look. Commissions matter at this sizing: they consumed ~85% of the session's gross.

## Who traded what

- **18:31–19:22 ET** — 4 bot momentum trades executed by the **Mac's local Playwright browser
  executor** (the CrossTrade webhook path deployed at 19:14 ET, commit `0055cd1`; the VPS has no
  Tradovate creds and no browser, so it could not trade before the deploy).
- **21:18–01:27 ET** — 7 bot momentum trades via the **VPS CrossTrade webhook path**
  (scale-out off; `$170` risk-budget sizing; market orders).
- **19:01/19:22** — 1 manual MES scalp (+$12.5).
- **08:39–08:55** — 4 manual MNQ trades, no signals in the DB and no bot log lines (+$477 gross).

## Signals vs fills — the bot's 11 overnight trades

| Signal | Dir | N | Signal entry/stop/tgt | Fill entry | Exit | Gross | Signal→fill Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 18:31 | L | 10 | 30796.25 / 30788.25 / 30804.25 | 30796.25 (limit, filled 11.6 min late) | 30804.25 TP | **+$160** | 0.00 |
| 18:44 | S | 18 | 30798.50 / 30803.00 / 30794.00 | 30798.50 | 30798.75 (covered 13 s later) | **−$9** | 0.00 |
| 18:47 | L | 28 | 30802.50 / 30799.50 / 30805.50 | 30798.50 | 5 @ 30796.0 SL + 23 @ 30802.0 TP | **+$136** | −4.00 |
| 19:15 | L | 14 | 30849.75 / 30843.75 / 30855.75 | 30847.00 (limit, filled 4.6 min late) | 30840.75 SL | **−$175** | −2.75 |
| 21:18 | L | 9 | 30844.75 / 30835.50 / 30854.00 | 30839.00 | 30832.6 SL | **−$115.5** | −5.75 |
| 22:26 | L | 10 | 30864.25 / 30856.25 / 30872.25 | 30863.50 | 30870.75 TP | **+$145** | +0.75 |
| 22:50 | S | 8 | 30882.50 / 30892.50 / 30872.50 | 30876.00 | 30888.53 SL | **−$200.5** | −6.50 |
| 23:08 | S | 8 | 30880.75 / 30890.50 / 30871.00 | 30881.00 | 30872.00 TP | **+$144** | −0.25 |
| 00:23 | L | 14 | 30898.00 / 30892.25 / 30903.75 | 30901.00 | 30906.25 TP | **+$147** | −3.00 |
| 00:41 | L | 9 | 30899.50 / 30890.75 / 30908.25 | 30897.75 | 30888.8 SL | **−$161.5** | +1.75 |
| 01:27 | S | 13 | 30887.25 / 30893.75 / 30880.75 | 30886.00 | 30891.00 SL | **−$130** | −1.25 |

Bot: 11 trades, 5W / 6L, **gross −$59.5** (wins +$732, losses −$791.5); ≈299 sides ⇒ ≈−$284
costs ⇒ bot net ≈ **−$343**. Manual trading (+$489.5 gross) carried the session to +$61.4 net.

## Why the 5 losses happened

### 1. 19:15 LONG 14 (−$175) — stopped at the exact low, then +70 pts
The browser path rolled a limit entry ("Buy Bid", 15% chance) → filled 4.6 min after the signal.
Stopped 19:21:06 at 30840.75 — the **low tick of the 19:21 bar** — and the market reversed there
and ran +70 pts to 30920 by 20:23. Direction was right; the stop was run at the flush extreme.
(Even with a perfect signal-price fill the stop would have been hit — this one is an in-model loss.)

### 2. 21:18 LONG 9 (−$115.5) — breakout straight into overhead congestion
Sequence: 21:15 failed flush (low 30822.5) → 21:18 breakout bar (76% buy, high 30847.75).
Fired 3 s after the close; market order filled at 30839 (already fading). The breakout entered the
30840–30858 congestion from the 20:30–20:59 range; sellers re-engaged the next minute (21:19 printed
a 16-pt down bar) and never looked back (30791.5 by 21:37). **Genuine failed breakout** — the
reference high it broke was inside a prior distribution, not above it.

### 3. 22:50 SHORT 8 (−$200.5) — counter-trend short of a buying climax
22:49 printed a 365-ct up bar to a new session high (30893.5); 22:50 reversed with an 82%-sell bar
→ expansion trigger shorted the reversal bar's close. But the night was a **one-way +110-pt
uptrend** (30816 → 30935), and 22:50 was the first counter-bar. The chop (22:51–22:58) then broke
back up through the stop. The expansion detector has **no trend/session-context filter**, so it
shorts (and longs) single huge counter-bars inside dominant trends — this is where its losses
concentrate.

### 4. 00:41 LONG 9 (−$161.5) — bought the exact double top, stopped at the exact low
00:41 bar high = 30899.50 = the 00:37 high to the tick (double top). Stopped 00:46 at
30888.75/30889 — the **low tick zone** — then the market reversed and ran +35 pts to 30935 by
01:02. Another stop-run at the extreme: entry at resistance, stop exactly at the probe low.

### 5. 01:27 SHORT 13 (−$130) — quote-anchored stop ran by 0.25 pt; would have been a winner
The failed-rally short fired at 30887.25 with the **structural stop at 30893.75** (breakout bar
high + 0.5). CrossTrade builds the bracket from its live reference quote at webhook arrival, not
from the signal stop: the effective stop landed at ≈30891.0. The bounce printed 01:29 high
**30891.25** — ran the quote-stop by 0.25 pt (fills 30891.0) — and the market then collapsed
15 pts to 30872.5 by 01:30 (target 30880.75). With the designed stop this trade wins +6.5 pts.
**A ~$300 swing caused purely by bracket anchoring.**

## Systemic findings (refinement targets)

1. **Bracket anchoring (biggest lever).** The webhook format is tick-based, so stops/targets are
   always `live-quote ± ticks`, never the signal's structural prices. Entry drift (median ~2 pts
   adverse on losers) shifts the whole bracket. Cost last night: flipped the 01:27 winner into a
   −$130 loss (−$299 swing), shrank the 22:26/23:08/00:23 winners by ≈$40, offset by ≈$51 saved on
   21:18 and ≈$40 on 22:50. Net ≈ −$250 vs designed brackets.
   Fix options: (a) REST place (`/v1/api/tv/accounts/{acct}/orders/place`) with **absolute**
   `stopLoss`/`takeProfit` at the signal prices; or (b) keep the webhook but attach our `order_id`
   to every entry and send a CHANGE to the structural stop right after the ack (the CHANGE path
   already exists for scale-out). Note: with the webhook, `require_market_position=flat` and
   isAutomated tagging stay; REST mutations bypass Alert History but keep the same broker gates.
2. **Expansion trigger needs a context filter.** Both expansion losses (22:50, 00:41) were entries
   into an extreme: one against the session trend, one at an exact double top. Candidates to
   backtest in the lab: require expansion direction == session cumulative-delta/VWAP side; veto
   entries whose bar high/low equals the prior swing extreme within 0.25; distance-to-overhead
   (prior POC/resistance stack) veto for failed-flush breakouts (the 21:18 case).
3. **Stop-run clustering.** 3 of 5 losses (19:15, 00:41, 01:27) were stopped within a tick of the
   exact swing extreme, and the market then moved hard in the trade direction. The signal-bar
   stop is the backtested optimum, so most of these are in-model — but check whether stop-runs
   cluster by hour/context (00:00–02:00 ET Globex?) or by trigger type (expansion vs failed-flush)
   in the 568-session replay before touching stop placement.
4. **Entry drift is asymmetric against us on losers.** On winners the market continues our way and
   we fill near the signal close; on losers it reverses in the 1–4 s before the market order lands
   and we fill worse. The backtest's close-price fill assumption overstates live expectancy by
   roughly the average adverse drift on losing trades. Quantify it in the lab (fill ≈ close ± first
   N seconds of the next bar) so live expectancy is forecast honestly.
5. **First-of-day discipline.** The 18:31 card (first of the session) won; the next 7 went 3W/4L —
   consistent with the 77.2% first-card vs ~74.5% rest split in the research. If fewer, better
   cards is preferred over more cards: consider trading only the first momentum card + A+ (both
   triggers) cards per session, or half size after the first. Trade-off: fewer signals, higher
   edge per signal.
6. **Playwright-era issues are closed** (path replaced by CrossTrade) but recorded: 15% random
   limit entries produced 11.6-min and 4.6-min delayed fills; the Tradovate ticket's persisted
   "Flatten" state covered the 18:44 short 13 s after entry (verify intent — it saved ≈$77 that
   time, but the behavior was uncontrolled); 2–3 min signal→order latency. None of these apply to
   the webhook path.
7. **Operational.** CrossTrade durable fill history (`/tv/fills/history`) was **empty** — journal
   capture is periodic (90 s debounce / 10 min interval / 5–6 pm ET window) and the Tradovate link
   was re-established at 19:01 ET; session-scoped lists (`/tv/fills`, `/tv/orders`) reset at the
   ~17:00 ET daily close. Verify Tradovate journal import is enabled in CrossTrade, and re-pull
   `/tv/fills/history` after 18:00 ET to confirm last night's fills got captured for the durable
   record.
8. **Data hygiene.** Store the A+ flag, the trigger bar, and the actual fill (entry/exit) on the
   signal row, or reconcile signals↔fills in a small nightly job — last night's post-mortem needed
   three systems (DB, CrossTrade API, container logs) to reconstruct. A `trades` table joined to
   `signals` would make these reviews a one-query job.

## Bottom line

Last night was a small-sample drawdown inside the model's noise band (11 trades; the 77% edge
produces 4–6 loss streaks regularly), with three fixable execution/concept leaks on top:
quote-anchored brackets (~−$250), expansion entries at extremes with no trend/context veto, and
entry drift against us on the trades that fail. The manual morning trading (+$477 gross) was the
only reason the session closed green after commissions. The momentum engine itself behaved as
designed: 5 of 6 losers were triggered correctly; the discipline question is which of the 7
post-open signals should have been skipped.

# Recovery runbook — new eval account, post-blow (2026-10-05)

> State: old eval (`MFFUEVREOD706880006`) blown. New eval
> (`MFFUEVREOD706880007`) is wired in Coolify env (runtime), clean at
> $50,000. Code fixes pushed to `main` (07d5f90), env changes saved,
> **emergency veto active** (`strategy_overrides` id 1: all families
> disabled) — the new account trades NOTHING until this runbook is walked.

## 1. Unblock Coolify's deploy queue (owner-side — needs dashboard or SSH)

Symptom: every deploy AND restart fails instantly with zero logs; the API
itself answers OK. The dashboard container still runs the old build.

1. Dashboard → **Settings → Restart Coolify** (restarts the queue worker).
   SSH equivalent: `docker restart coolify` on the VPS.
2. Check disk (a full disk fails deploys exactly like this):
   `ssh root@31.97.138.30 'df -h /'` — free space needed for the build.
3. Dashboard → **nq-dashboard → Redeploy** (pulls 07d5f90). This applies
   the new code AND the saved env together.

## 2. Verify the deploy (any reader can check the health endpoint)

```
curl https://nq-dashboard.31.97.138.30.sslip.io/api/gc?action=health
```

All of these must flip before proceeding:
- `execution.liveFeed.barSource` exists (new build live — candle-synced bars)
- `execution.feeds.momentum == false`
- `execution.protections` shows the giveback guard + (floor knob is env-only;
  verify in Coolify: `DAILY_LOSS_FLOOR=400`, `RTH_MAX_CARDS_PER_DAY=3`,
  `RTH_PROFILE=0`, `CROSSTRADE_ACCOUNT=MFFUEVREOD706880007`)

## 3. Watch one session with the veto ON

Zero cards may fire (the veto must hold). Check:
`select * from strategy_overrides;` → id 1 active=true.
The signals table may record veto skips — that is the veto working.

## 4. Lift the veto

```sql
update strategy_overrides set active = false where id = 1;
```

## 5. Resume with the approved config (journal everything)

- RTH only: structural 0.75R brackets, max 3 cards/day, −$400/day floor.
- Momentum/expansion stay OFF until drift is re-measured (F3: no passing
  cell at measured frictions).
- Journal the first ~10 cards against the F3 baselines (RTH structural
  first-3: +4.28 pts/trade, 16/16 walk-forward).

## 6. Operations that keep it from happening again

- **Nightly tape parity** (ships with the new build): snapshot the
  live-written bars before ingest, diff vs the vendor archive, one
  `tape_parity` row per night. A diverging tape is the alarm.
- **Re-measure live friction** after a few sessions (entry drift, realized
  cost per trade) → re-run `scripts/gapOnlyValidation.ts` → only then
  reconsider `FEED_MOMENTUM=1` (approval path).
- **The veto is the emergency brake**: one DB row stops all cards without
  a deploy. Use it at the first sign of tape/execution divergence.

## 7. Emergency brake (pull any time)

```sql
insert into strategy_overrides (family, gate, value, active, note)
values ('all','enable','{"enabled":false}',true,'emergency halt');
```

# Cheaper MyFundedFutures Alternatives on the Same Stack (Tradovate via CrossTrade)

Research date: 2026-10-05. Sources are cross-checked between CrossTrade's firm
guides (reviewed Sep 23, 2026), PropScorer live data (Oct 5, 2026), firm help
centers, Tradecopia, TradersPost, and independent reviews (The Industry Spread).

## 1. The constraint is not "Tradovate", it's "CrossTrade → Tradovate cloud"

Our executor (`web/lib/crossTrade.ts`) places orders through the CrossTrade
cloud REST path with `destination=tradovate` and an `isAutomated` flag. The
binding requirements for a drop-in swap are therefore:

1. The firm's Tradovate instance can be linked in CrossTrade and supports
   **direct cloud routing** (`destination=tradovate`, no NT8 Add-On).
2. The firm **permits automated order entry** from your own system.
3. Rules that don't break the NQ/MNQ scalping profile (EOD drawdown ≫ intraday
   trailing, sane consistency rules, micros allowed, no HFT/microscalping bans
   we'd trip).

CrossTrade's own directory covers exactly 9 firms. Filtered to Tradovate-cloud
+ automation-friendly, the real candidates are **Lucid Trading**, **BluSky**,
and (with conditions) **Tradeify**. Everything else either fails the automation
policy or the cloud-routing requirement — including the usual "cheapest" answer,
Apex.

## 2. Candidates ruled out (important)

| Firm | Why it fails for our stack |
| --- | --- |
| **Apex Trader Funding** (cheapest with 80–90% off promos) | User Agreement requires **manual order entry**; bots/scripts/strategies that place or modify orders from signals are prohibited on eval AND PA accounts. Only manual-entry + mirror-copying is allowed. Incompatible with our automated executor. ([CrossTrade Apex guide](https://crosstrade.io/prop-firms/apex-trader-funding)) |
| **Take Profit Trader** | Automated trading not permitted; only TPT-approved copiers. |
| **Earn2Trade** | Trade copiers not allowed on any program; automation murky. |
| **Bulenox** | CrossTrade lists it as **Rithmic-only** — no Tradovate cloud route. |
| **TradeDay** | Automation allowed (own strategies), but **no Tradovate API for automated systems** — needs the NT8 desktop Add-On route. That's a stack change (Windows/NT8 dependency), not a drop-in. |
| **TopStep / TickTick / FastTrack / MyFlashFunding / FundedNext etc.** | Not in CrossTrade's covered Tradovate set (TopStep now pushes TopStepX; others are Rithmic/other). Would require rewriting the execution layer. |

## 3. Shortlist comparison (50K tier, discounted where known)

| | **MFFU Builder 50K (current)** | **Lucid Flex 50K** ⭐ | **BluSky Propel 50K** | **Tradeify Growth 50K** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Eval cost | $153 list / **$107** (30%) / $92 (40%, 2 uses) | $146 list / **$102.20** (code LAB 30%) | subscription, ~$59–79/30d (renews until pass; discount persists) | ~$99+ |
| Recurring | one-time | one-time | **monthly until you pass** | one-time |
| Activation | $0 | $0 | $0 | $0 |
| Reset | ~$99-ish | $90 (50K) | $79 (or free on renewal) | n/a |
| Profit target | $3,000 | $3,000 | $3,000 | $3,000 |
| Drawdown | EOD trailing $2,000, locks at start+$100 | EOD trailing $2,000, locks at start+$100 | EOD trailing $2,000 | EOD trailing $2,000 |
| DLL | $1,000 soft | optional, $1,200 or off (choose at purchase, free) | none | $1,250 soft |
| Consistency | none in eval; 50% on payouts | **50% eval only, 0% once funded (Flex)** | 34% (best day ÷ sum of profitable days) | none in eval; 35% funded |
| Min days | 1 | 1 | 3 profitable days implied by consistency | 1 |
| Max contracts | 4 mini / 40 micro | 4 mini / 40 micro | 5 mini / 50 micro | ~6 mini (verify) |
| Split | 80/20 | **90/10** | 90/10 | 90/10 |
| Payout cadence | 48h after first trade; cap $2k/cycle; max 5 sim payouts → live | any day after criteria; Flex needs 5 profitable days/cycle; ~15 min processing | daily (before 11am ET same day); $250 min | weekly-ish (verify) |
| News trading | allowed | allowed (Flex/Pro/Direct) | allowed | allowed |
| Max funded accts | 1 sim funded at a time | **5 funded + 10 evals** | 3 funded | 5 funded |
| Automation | allowed (we flag isAutomated) | **explicitly allowed** (not HFT; no >50% of profit from ≤5s holds) | bots + micro-scalping allowed | allowed with conditions (see below) |
| CrossTrade cloud Tradovate route | ✅ (current) | ✅ no Add-On | ✅ no Add-On | ✅ no Add-On |

**Reading the "cheaper" question honestly:** at the 50K tier, list prices are
all in the same $100–150 band — nobody is dramatically cheaper at checkout than
MFFU's promos. The real savings are structural: Lucid pays **90/10 vs MFFU's
80/20** (+12.5% on every payout), has **no consistency rule once funded** (Flex),
no 5-payout cap, up to 5 funded accounts, and cheapest entry of the viable set
at the 25K tier (**$62.30** Flex / **$73.80** Pro with codes). BluSky's
subscription is the cheapest *if you pass in month one*; it compounds against
you the longer evaluation takes, and its 4-stage funnel adds a second profit
target (Buffer Zone) before withdrawals.

## 4. Lucid Trading — top pick for our stack (verify before buying)

- **Identical architecture to current setup.** "Link your Lucid Tradovate login
  for direct cloud routing with `destination=tradovate` and no Add-On" — the
  exact path `web/lib/crossTrade.ts` uses. Swap = link account in CrossTrade +
  change `CROSSTRADE_ACCOUNT`. Same Tradovate backend → same NQ/MNQ one-digit
  year symbols, same bracket/OCO semantics our executor relies on.
- **Automation explicitly permitted** on eval and funded accounts (CrossTrade's
  "For automation" pick). Hard lines: high-frequency trading, **microscalping
  defined as >50% of profits from trades held ≤5 seconds**, hedging across
  accounts, red-folder news on LucidDaily only. Our bracket-managed scalping
  (minute-scale holds per the trade reviews) should be fine, but confirm hold-
  time distribution before committing.
- **Rules fit the strategy:** EOD trailing drawdown that permanently locks at
  starting balance + $100 (same mechanic as MFFU Builder) → intraday NQ
  round-trips can't trap us; DLL optional (take the no-DLL version and keep our
  own CrossTrade guard); 50% consistency only during Flex eval, gone once funded;
  4:45pm ET flat rule matches our existing EOD flatten config.
- Pricing (Tradecopia, current codes): Flex 25K $62.30 / 50K $102.20 / 100K
  $205.10 (code LAB 30%). Pro 50K **$115.20** with 40% code COPIA. Direct
  (no eval) 50K $360.50. One-time, no recurring, $0 activation.
- Trust: Trustpilot 4.7 (~3,200 reviews — small base), est. early 2025, 90/10
  split upgraded from 80/20 in Mar 2026, payouts independently reported at
  ~15 min processing. **Flags:** youngest firm in the set; unverified
  registration jurisdiction (Lucid Prop Ltd); sources conflict on whether the
  split steps down to 80/20 at the LucidLive (real-capital) stage — get this in
  writing before scaling; isolated EliteTrader complaint thread of a trader
  dropped after 4 payouts (rule-violation pattern, unverified).

## 5. BluSky — runner-up (cheap-to-start, but read the funnel)

- Cloud Tradovate route works; bots and micro-scalping allowed; static-drawdown
  plans (150K: $1,000 static DD / $3,000 target) are the most forgiving
  structure in this set for scalping; 34% consistency denominator is gentler
  (best day ÷ sum of *profitable* days, losing days ignored).
- **Cost model is a subscription** (~$59–79/30 days, your discounted price
  renews verbatim, stops when you pass; failed-account renewal includes a free
  reset; standalone reset $79). Cheap for a fast pass, expensive for a slow one.
- **Four stages:** Evaluation → Buffer Zone (its own target + consistency, resets
  $250) → Sim Funded → Live Brokerage. Only Live Brokerage touches real markets;
  trigger is $10,000 total profit, max $10K/account live, $30K/trader; profit
  above $10K pre-review is not payable; trading during a review is the #1
  account-killer; broker rejection forfeits everything. Fine as a cheap strategy
  testbed; think hard before treating Sim Funded payouts as the end goal.
- Trust: est. 2022, TP ~4.5 (899 reviews), payout transparency limited; its own
  marketing blog contradicts its help center in places — trust the help center.

## 6. Tradeify — only if Lucid/BluSky fall through

Cloud Tradovate route OK, EOD trailing, news allowed, 5 funded accounts, no
eval consistency on Growth. But its automation conditions are onerous for a
team repo: strategy must be **solely owned by you**, not used at other firms,
not shared, and they may demand a **live video proving ownership** of the code.
Plus 35% funded consistency. A compliance headache we don't need while MFFU,
Lucid, and BluSky are all friendlier.

## 7. Integration swap effort (Lucid path)

1. Buy Lucid eval (smallest size first: 25K Flex $62.30 or 50K Flex $102.20),
   sign into Lucid's Tradovate with the Lucid credentials (their setup flow).
2. In CrossTrade: link the Lucid Tradovate account (under Demo), same as the MFF
   link; set `CROSSTRADE_ACCOUNT` to the Lucid account name. No code changes
   expected in `web/lib/crossTrade.ts` — same `destination=tradovate` path.
3. Confirm with Lucid support **in writing**: (a) automated order entry via a
   linked third-party bridge (CrossTrade) is permitted, (b) the 90/10 split at
   every stage including any LucidLive program, (c) whether the ≤5s-hold
   microscalping threshold applies to our hold-time profile.
4. Keep the MFFU account untouched as the A/B control; run the same signal
   stream to both for a week and compare fills/slippage in the journal.

## 8. Recommendation

**Primary: Lucid Trading (Flex, EOD drawdown, no-DLL version).** Only firm that
matches our current architecture one-to-one, explicitly allows our automation
model, has the most scalper-friendly rule stack of the affordable set (locked
EOD drawdown, no funded consistency on Flex), and pays 90/10. Use 25K or 50K
with the LAB code for the cheapest viable entry.

**Secondary: BluSky Propel 50K** if we want the absolute lowest first-month
cash outlay (~$59) and can pass quickly; accept the subscription renewal risk
and treat it as a testbed, not a payout vehicle, until the Live Brokerage stage
is actually shipped and reviewed.

**Avoid Apex despite the price** — its manual-order-entry rule makes our
executor a bannable offense, not a workflow.

# Medallion-inspired experiment ideas (2026-10-07)

**Trigger:** FINAiUS documentary "The Greatest Moneymaker in History"
(analysis: `docs/research/medallion-documentary-2026-10-07.md`, transcript:
`transcripts/8j3Oauy4IRc_transcript.txt`).

**Contract (same as the Naso plan):** every idea below is a *hypothesis*.
Nothing gates a live feed until a study passes its pre-registered acceptance
criteria, survives a 2026-01-01 train/test split, and lands as a playbook
entry + feed flag. Journal-only chips first, always.

**The thesis in one line:** Medallion's repeatable parts — breadth
accounting, Kelly-consistent sizing to measured edge, ensemble blending of
weak signals, residual (market-neutral) construction, state inference,
forced-flow capture, capacity honesty — each has a direct, falsifiable
experiment on the existing 649-session NQ archive. Seven are below, ranked.

---

## 1. Breadth audit — how many *independent* bets are we really making?

**Medallion principle:** IR = IC × √N, and you need ~17,000 *independent*
bets to be 95% sure a 50.75% edge is real. Correlated trades don't count.
Our momentum card claims 77.5% WR over 4,822 trades (~7.4/day) — but how
many effective independent bets is that? The per-year wobble (2024 80.0% ·
2025 75.3% · 2026 77.9%) may be exactly the noise the documentary warns
about.

**Experiment — `web/scripts/breadthAudit.ts`:**
- From the sequential replay outcomes, compute lag-1/2/3 autocorrelation
  of win/loss (and of $ outcomes) within each day, and the same-day
  correlation structure across card families (momentum ↔ RTH ↔ open).
- Estimate the *effective N* per day (e.g., variance-inflation factor or
  block bootstrap) and the resulting 95% CI on the true WR/PF.
- Output: "trading days needed to prove this edge at 95%" per family, and
  a per-family independence table.

**Pre-registered acceptance:** descriptive study — publishes the effective
N and the CI. *Behavior changes* only if any family's effective N is so
low that its measured PF is not distinguishable from PF 1.0 at 95%
(sizing would then be reviewed, not the signal).

**Why fun:** this is the Medallion arithmetic applied to the one number we
trust most — and the answer tells us how much of our edge is breadth vs luck.

---

## 2. Kelly-flavored sizing: size to the *measured cell edge*, not flat $100

**Medallion principle:** Kelly — bet fraction ≈ measured edge per bet;
size up where the measured edge is bigger (Berlekamp's 1989 fix was
literally re-sizing to arithmetic). We already have measured per-cell
edges: `ES CONFIRM` 85.2% / PF 4.84, `FOMC DAY` 83.8% / PF 5.16,
`HOUR 3–7 ET` 79.8% / PF 3.27 vs the 77.5% / 2.98 baseline. Today those
cells are labels — and every card risks the same flat $100.

**Experiment — `web/scripts/kellySizingStudy.ts`:**
- For each measured chip cell (and the A+ tier), compute a *shrunk* edge
  estimate (train window only; shrinkage toward the family mean — the
  documentary's regularization).
- Map edge → risk-per-trade: `risk$ = clamp(edge_share × K × budget, 100, cap)`
  with K ≈ 0.25–0.5 Kelly equivalent (their −$250 floor and MLL are the
  bounds; 30-micro cap the ceiling).
- Replay the exact MFF sim comparing flat $100 vs cell-scaled sizing.

**Pre-registered acceptance:** cell-scaled sizing passes only if it
(a) improves median eval-day P&L or funded payout path, and (b) does not
raise funded blow rate (flat is 0.3%, 0.0% with the dd rule) and (c) the
improvement survives the train/test split. Otherwise → reject; chips stay
labels.

**Why fun:** it converts the whole chip zoo from trivia into a sizing
engine — Medallion's exact move — with the prop rules as the Kelly bound.

---

## 3. Chip blending → one score (the ensemble test)

**Medallion principle:** 100 signals, each 0.02-correlated with the next
move, blend to ~0.2; one forecast per market, orders netted. We have ~10
measured weak features sitting in `signals.features` jsonb (ES chips,
seasonal chips, round/gap/wall labels, A+ tier). Never combined.

**Experiment — `web/scripts/chipBlendStudy.ts`:**
- Train window (through 2025-12-31): fit a *simple* log-odds blend
  (logistic regression, L2 regularization — the "simple regression done
  right" the documentary credits) of the chip features to win/loss.
- Test window: score every card; report outcome by decile.
- Compare: top-decile vs bottom-decile vs single-best-chip (ES CONFIRM)
  vs baseline.

**Pre-registered acceptance:** the blend only matters if the top decile
beats *both* the baseline and the single best chip on OOS PF/WR with
n ≥ ~80, and the bottom decile is skippable without hurting session
coverage. Anything less → chips remain labels (multiple-testing is the
null here; the documentary says most blends of this kind are false).

**Why fun:** this is the "one model" doctrine in miniature — and if the
weak chips really carry 0.02-ish correlations, the top decile should be
visibly better than any single chip.

---

## 4. NQ/ES residual — trade the part the market doesn't explain

**Medallion principle:** strip market/industry/factor moves, trade the
residual; "related contracts pull back together after drifting apart"
(the gold/silver ghost); ~zero beta construction. We have the ES twin
feed wired already (`web/lib/esJoin.ts`) and an `RS STRETCH` chip.

**Two experiments — `web/scripts/nqEsResidualStudy.ts`:**
- **(a) Residual triggers:** re-run MOM_PROD/EXP_PROD with each NQ bar's
  move replaced by its residual vs ES (NQ% − β·ES% over a trailing
  window). Do residual breakouts beat raw-price breakouts?
- **(b) Divergence reversion:** when NQ and ES cumulative deltas/returns
  drift apart over 30–60 bars, measure whether the gap narrows (and with
  what WR/PF using existing card mechanics on the convergence side).

**Pre-registered acceptance:** either variant passes only with n ≥ ~100,
WR/PF ≥ baseline, and 2026-01-01 OOS survival. Journal-only otherwise.

**Why fun:** the closest thing to Medallion's actual book (5,000 long /
5,000 short, market-neutral) reachable with our two feeds — and it could
produce a genuinely new card family.

---

## 5. Forced-flow capture cells — where does the "house" trade pay?

**Medallion principle:** the house gets paid for absorbing urgent flow.
Our liquidity-provision trade is the expansion retrace arm (`EXP_RETRACE`:
resting limit 1 pt behind the close — 68% WR, PF 1.29). The market entry
is PF 3.14; the capture is where we give it back. Where is the capture
edge best?

**Experiment — `web/scripts/retraceCaptureStudy.ts`:** bucket EXP_RETRACE
by (a) hour band (thin overnight vs thick RTH), (b) round-number proximity
(chips already logged), (c) bar size above the 1.6×ATR gate (1.6–2× vs
2×+), (d) wall proximity when logged. Report fill rate, WR, PF per cell.

**Pre-registered acceptance:** a cell must beat the 68% / 1.29 baseline
with n ≥ ~100 before the retrace arm's TTLS or size is made cell-conditional.
Negative cells → the arm shrinks its risk there (capacity honesty in
reverse: don't provide liquidity where it isn't paid).

**Why fun:** this is the direct "casino/house" experiment — it finds the
tables where our house edge is actually positive.

---

## 6. State inference (HMM-lite): size to the hidden "mood"

**Medallion principle:** IDA 1964 — model the market as hidden states
(quiet/stormy), infer the state with Baum–Welch/EM, and shrink bets the
moment the evidence flips. We have vol gates and dd rules, but no
explicit state estimate.

**Experiment — `web/scripts/regimeStateStudy.ts`:**
- Fit a 2–3 state Gaussian HMM on 5-min NQ log-returns (quiet / normal /
  stormy), train window only; infer the smoothed state at every card
  entry; bucket outcomes by state.
- Cheap proxy control: trailing 20-bar range percentile (extend rather
  than duplicate `vol-sizing-study-2026-10-04.md` if it covers this).

**Pre-registered acceptance:** a state cell must be materially worse
(e.g., the PRE-FOMC pattern: ~67% vs 82%) with n ≥ ~100 and OOS survival
before a stand-aside or half-size rule is proposed. The null is "our
existing ATR/DD machinery already does this job."

**Why fun:** it's the documentary's origin story (codebreakers) turned
into a 2-3 state model on our own tape — and it tests whether our vol
gates are leaving state information on the table.

---

## 7. Capacity table + decay watch (process, near-zero code)

**Medallion principles:** (a) the cap is arithmetic — each strategy has a
max size where impact eats the edge; (b) edges decay 5–10 years — "if you
don't keep getting better, you're going to do worse."

- **Capacity table:** per card family, sweep contracts 1→30 through the
  MFF sim and publish the max contracts before funded blow degrades —
  a formal "capacity ceiling" line per strategy in the playbook
  (open family already says "never scale"; give every family its number,
  including EXP_RETRACE and the A+ tier).
- **Decay watch:** rolling 100-trade WR/PF control chart on the live
  journal; a Telegram heads-up (journal-only, per the no-noise rule)
  when the rolling window drops >2σ below the archive baseline. The
  per-year table (80.0 / 75.3 / 77.9) already wobbles — this makes the
  wobble *actionable* before it costs money.
- **False-discovery ledger:** count every hypothesis this repo has tested
  (the research docs *are* the ledger), estimate expected false
  discoveries at 1%, and raise the bar for any future gate accordingly.
  One doc, no code. It is the Patterson defense applied to our own repo.

**Acceptance:** these ship as docs/alerts; the decay watch's threshold is
pre-registered before it can ever suggest a feed flag.

---

## Ranked by expected value ÷ effort

| # | Idea | Medallion piece | Cost | Expected value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Breadth audit | IR = IC×√N, 17k-bet proof | 1 script | High — calibrates trust in every number we have |
| 3 | Chip blend → one score | Ensembling / one model | 1 script | High — first real use of the chip zoo |
| 2 | Cell-edge Kelly sizing | Kelly / Berlekamp re-sizing | 1 script + sweep | High — turns labels into a sizing engine |
| 4 | NQ/ES residual | Market-neutral, ghosts | 1–2 scripts | Medium-high — potential new card family |
| 5 | Retrace capture cells | The house trade | 1 script | Medium — sharpens the only negative-PF live arm |
| 6 | HMM state inference | Hidden states, size to mood | 1 script | Medium — may duplicate existing vol machinery |
| 7 | Capacity table + decay watch + FDR ledger | Cap is arithmetic; decay; multiple testing | Docs + tiny code | Medium — durable process value |

All seven are pre-registered falsifiable studies in the house style; say
the word and I'll start with #1 (or any other).

# Medallion Documentary — Analysis & Extractable Learnings

- **Video:** [The Greatest Moneymaker in History | Full Documentary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8j3Oauy4IRc) — FINAiUS, ~54 min, uploaded 2026-10-06
- **Subject:** Renaissance Technologies' Medallion Fund — the best documented trading record in history
- **Transcript:** `transcripts/8j3Oauy4IRc_transcript.txt` (verbatim, auto-generated; name corrections below)
- **Analyzed:** 2026-10-07

---

## 1. TL;DR

Medallion is not a story about a magical signal. It is a story about **arithmetic done relentlessly**:

1. A **tiny edge** (~50.75% win rate — barely better than a coin flip) that is *measured, not guessed*.
2. **Enormous breadth** — 100,000+ trades/day, ~30M/year — which turns an unprovable edge into a statistically *proven* one (Fundamental Law of Active Management).
3. **Kelly-consistent sizing** — ~1.5% of capital per bet at that edge; never over-bet.
4. **Obsessive data hygiene** — clean data, out-of-sample testing, shrinkage — so the firm never trades a backtest artifact.
5. **One blended model** — thousands of weak signals netted into one forecast per market (cost saving + ensemble effect).
6. **Short horizons + leverage + market-neutral construction** — absorb forced flow, carry ~zero market beta.
7. **Capacity honesty** — the fund is capped (~$10B) and pays out every 6 months because impact costs grow faster than profits. The cap is arithmetic, not modesty.

The five public parts of the machine (clean data, thousands of weak signals, one model, short holding periods, borrowed money) are all known. **The combination is the edge.**

---

## 2. Key facts & numbers (as stated in the video)

| Fact | Figure |
|---|---|
| Average gross return 1988–2018 | ~66%/yr before fees, ~39%/yr after (Zuckerman) |
| Fees (2017 filing) | as high as 5% AUM + 44% of profits |
| $100 in 1988, compounded, by 2018 | ~$398.7M before fees (Cornell 2019) |
| Sharpe ratio | > 2 (multi-decade; ~1 is "very good") |
| Beta to stock market | **negative** — profits don't come from market direction |
| Recalculated return (payout-adjusted) | ~31.8%/yr before fees, "probably under 35%" (Gu & Liu 2024) |
| Win rate | 50.75% ("right 50.75% of the time, 100% right 50.75% of the time" — Mercer) |
| Trades/day (Senate PSI report, 2014) | >100,000/day, ~30M/yr; some positions last seconds |
| Holding profile | 97% of holdings sold within 6 months |
| Leverage via basket options | up to $20 of stock per $1 of capital (Deutsche Bank 2000, Barclays 2002) |
| Profits 2000–2013 through basket accounts | ~$34B; Senate estimated ~$6.8B tax avoided |
| IRS settlement (Sept 2021) | up to $7B by 7 current/former board members + spouses; Simons +$670M — largest tax settlement on record |
| Medallion size cap | ~$10B (Bloomberg); profits paid out ~every 6 months |
| Aug 2007 "quant quake" | Medallion −$1B+ in one week (~20% of value); RIEF ~−$3B (~10%) |
| 2020 split | Medallion **+76%** vs RIEF **−19%**, diversified fund **−32%** |
| 2024 | Medallion ~+30% (Zuckerman); Oct 2025: both outside funds −15% in a month; RIEF shrunk to <$20B from ~$36B at start of 2020 |
| Virtu clip (for contrast) | won every day for ~1,300 days except one — the one loss was a computer problem |

---

## 3. ASR name corrections (the transcript garbles proper nouns)

| "Bomb Welch algorithm", "Leonard Bal", "Lenny Bal" | **Baum–Welch algorithm**, Leonard **Baum** (EM family) |

| "Henry Laugher / Loer" | Henry **Laufer** (5-minute slicing) |
| "Richard Grenold" | Richard **Grinold** (Fundamental Law of Active Management, 1989) |
| "Bas's rule" | **Bayes'** rule |
| "hidden Marov model" | hidden **Markov** model |
| "David Maghermanman / Megererman / Megman / Meerman" | David **Magerman** |
| "Pavo Vulb", "Alexander Bellapolski" | Pavel **Volfbeyn**, Alexander **Belopolsky** |
| "Amir Kandani" | Amir **Khandani** (Khandani & Lo 2007) |
| "Bruce Layman, Andrew Low, Craig McKinley" | Lehmann (1990); Lo & MacKinlay (1990) |

| "Stimmans Foundation" | **Simons** Foundation |
| "sharp ratio" | **Sharpe** ratio |

---

## 4. The arithmetic of a coin flip — the core of the video

The video's most important chapter. Three pillars:

### 4.1 Proof — frequency turns edge into certainty
At 50.75% win rate, you need **~17,000 independent bets** to be 95% sure the edge is real and not luck. A fund holding positions for months makes a few dozen independent bets a year — it can *never* prove its edge. A fund trading in and out daily proves it **within months**. Fast turnover is not just profit per trade — it's the *epistemology* of trading: the only way to know your edge is real.

### 4.2 Breadth — the Fundamental Law
Grinold (1989): risk-adjusted return ≈ skill × √(number of independent bets).
- Double skill → double the result. Quadruple bets → also double.
- 50.75% skill: 10,000 bets/yr → information ratio ≈ 1.5 (already excellent); 100,000 bets/yr → IR ≈ 4.7.
- Lesson: **breadth is a lever equal in power to skill**, and far easier to increase. The catch: bets must be *independent* (uncorrelated outcomes), not 100,000 repetitions of one correlated view.

### 4.3 Sizing — Kelly
Kelly (1956): for an even-money bet, the optimal fraction of capital = edge = win% − loss% = 1.5% at 50.75%.
- Bet less → growth slows gently. Bet **2× Kelly** → long-run growth → 0. Bet more → even a real edge loses capital.
- Berlekamp's 1989 turnaround diagnosis was literally: *the trades were sized wrong*. Fix = smaller, faster, far more numerous bets.
- Medallion's near-death (Aug 2007) is framed as the same Kelly lesson in reverse: borrowed money made losses 2–3× bigger than the edge could bear.

**Practical translation:** at a ~50.75% even-money edge, risk ~0.75–1.5% per independent bet (half-to-full Kelly). The workspace's existing sizing studies (`docs/research/sizing-*.md`) are the same problem in disguise.

---

## 5. How not to fool yourself — the anti-overfit doctrine

This is the most directly stealable chapter for anyone with a backtesting pipeline.

**Defense 1 — Clean data.** One bad print ($10 stock recorded at $100 for a single trade) looks like a spike-and-snap-back — exactly what a mean-reversion system loves. Dirty data **manufactures fake profits**. Renaissance assigned several PhDs to do nothing but clean vendor data. (Our tick data / `gcdata` is the same battle.)

**Defense 2 — Skepticism about luck (multiple testing).** Test 10,000 random ideas at 1% significance → ~100 pass by chance alone. "Most strategies presented to an investment committee are false discoveries as a result of selection bias and multiple testing." A signal only survives if it works on **unseen data**, across **different markets and years**, and survives **shrinkage** (conservatively estimated strength). Patterson: the firm's most important tool was **simple regression done right**.

**Defense 3 — One single model.** Thousands of weak signals feed ONE system, blended into one forecast per market:
- 100 independent signals, each 0.02 correlated with next move (indistinguishable from noise) → together ~0.2. Real signals overlap, so the true gain is smaller — ensemble effect.
- One model **nets orders**: signal A says buy 1,000, signal B says sell 800 → trade 200, not 1,800. Separate strategies would pay costs on all 1,800.
- One shared model also aligns incentives: every researcher improves the same system; no fiefdoms.

Today these have ML names: data cleaning, out-of-sample testing, regularization (shrinkage), ensembling.

---

## 6. The stock engine — what it actually trades

Public descriptions (Magerman's account, the clearest public one):

- **Residual reversion / stat-arb.** Strip out what market, industry, and factors (size etc.) explain; trade the **residual** — the move that belongs to that stock alone. Large residuals tend to shrink over hours/days.
- **Pairs logic:** two regional banks fall on the same news — one −3%, one −1%, nothing new explains the bigger drop → **buy the bigger loser, short the smaller loser**, bet the gap narrows.
- **Scale:** ~5,000 stocks long, ~5,000 short; every purchase hedged by a bet against something similar → market direction barely matters (matches Cornell's finding of ~zero/negative beta).
- **Frequency:** positions adjusted roughly **every 15 minutes**.
- **Leverage:** $4.5–$7 of stock per $1 of capital (later $20 via basket options).
- **Framing:** "Renaissance was a casino, and they were the house" — the law of large numbers pays the house. The *edge* is being the house: absorbing forced flow (a pension fund dumping a block must accept a worse price; whoever takes the other side gets paid).
- The idea is 30+ years old and public (Lehmann 1990; Lo & MacKinlay 1990: buy recent losers, short recent winners). **The public idea + their combination is not.**

This is exactly the territory of the project's stop-run/liquidity-sweep and reversal-vs-fakeout research: getting paid to absorb *forced* order flow.

---

## 7. Capacity, impact, and the two-clock split

- **Square-root impact law:** impact/share grows with √(order size). Quadruple the order → each share costs ~2× more. Even 1% of ADV moves price ~10% of daily volatility. So the system trades **only partway toward targets** when signal < cost of acting.
- **Profit = edge × money traded − cost of trading.** Costs grow faster than money → at some size, more money = **less** profit. Hence: the ~$10B cap and the 6-month payouts. "The cap is not modesty. It is arithmetic."
- **Signal decay:** Simons — signals erode within 5–10 years as others discover them. "If you don't keep getting better, you're going to do worse."
- **Crowding:** by the mid-2000s many quant funds held the same book; one big unwind → forced selling cascade (Aug 2007: indexes barely moved while quant longs fell and shorts rose).
- **Two funds, two clocks:** short-horizon signals = more accurate, tiny capacity; long-horizon = weaker edge, huge capacity. Renaissance's outside funds (RIEF 2005, diversified 2012) run the longer clock. 2020 made the split brutal: Medallion +76% vs RIEF −19%, RIDEF −32%; outside clients fled while insiders *added* money. A short-term trader profits from chaos (more forced sellers, bigger mispricings); a long-horizon fund gets caught on the wrong side for months.
- **Why it matters to us:** this is the fundamental trade-off of scalping vs swing. Short horizons have the strongest, fastest-provable edge — and hard capacity limits. Most of the project's size-cap research is this exact law.

---

## 8. Failure & survival lessons (the video's "crash" chapters)

1. **1989–90 turnaround:** trend-following with weeks-long holds lost money; Berlekamp's fix was arithmetic (shorter, smaller, more bets, short side enabled). +55.9% after fees in 1990. *The edge was in the structure, not a better trend signal.*
2. **LTCM contrast (1998):** same reversion logic, but slow bets with **no defined payoff time-scale**, plus heavy leverage → forced liquidation. Simons' line: their bets "have no clear time scale for when they pay off." Most Medallion bets resolve **within days**. *Speed is a risk-management tool, not just a profit tool.*
3. **Aug 2007 quant quake:** crowded books + leverage = contagion. Medallion lost $1B+/week (~20%); Magerman: "another week would have put the firm out of business." Even the house gets caught in panics.
4. **The human-hand paradox:** Simons overrode the model and cut positions — the market snapped back, and staff later complained the override **cost them gains**. Yet in 2008 he pulled money from a shaky counterparty *before* trouble ("they wouldn't have requested the meeting unless they were in real trouble"). Lesson: the system beats instinct for *signals*; instinct beat the system for *counterparty survival*. Keep the two separated.
5. **People risk:** two MIT physicists defected to Millennium with the methods (2003) → lawsuit, $20M settlement, non-competes. Edge = code + data + people; protect all three.
6. **Tax/legal risk is real P&L:** the basket-option structure (delta-1 options on bank accounts, 40-second holds taxed as long-term gains) bought $6.8B of tax savings but ended in the largest tax settlement in history (~$7B), a 7-year public fight, and reputational damage. *Structural/regulatory risk compounds silently.*
7. **Ownership alignment:** Medallion kicked out outside investors from 1993; ~70% of the firm held by the top 5 executives; staff bonus pool = half of net income; employees pay the 5/44 fees to their own firm. The incentives and the strategy are one system.

---

## 9. What we can extract (prioritized)

### A. General trading principles
1. **Optimize expectancy × breadth, not accuracy.** 50.75% is enough if it's real and repeated 100,000×/day. Stop chasing high win rates; chase *measured edge per trade × independent trades per year*.
2. **Frequency is proof.** At ~51% edge you need ~17,000 independent bets for statistical certainty. Intraday/scalping horizons are the only place a small edge can be *validated* within a career — and within a backtest.
3. **IR ≈ IC × √N.** More *independent* bets raise risk-adjusted return as powerfully as more skill. Correlated trades do not count as new bets (don't count 20 entries in one trend as 20 bets).
4. **Kelly sizing.** Risk ≈ edge per bet (1.5% at 50.75% even-money); never > 2× Kelly; half-Kelly is the practical default. Overbetting converts a real edge into guaranteed ruin.
5. **Signal must pay a defined time-scale.** If you can't say *when* a bet pays off, it can be liquidated before it does (LTCM). Short-horizon signals resolve in days — the model's own stop-clock.
6. **Be the house, not the player.** Get paid to absorb forced flow (blocks, stops, liquidations, panics). The stop-run/sweep research in this repo is the same trade in scalper form.
7. **Short horizons = strongest alpha, smallest capacity.** Size caps and profit payouts are arithmetic (square-root impact law), not modesty.
8. **Edges decay (5–10 yrs).** Continuous research is a survival requirement, not a bonus.

### B. Backtest/research hygiene (directly applicable to this repo)
9. **Clean data before signal hunting.** Bad prints manufacture fake reversion signals. (Patterson: vendor data is "full of trash"; PhDs cleaned it.)
10. **Multiple-testing budget.** 10,000 tests at 1% → ~100 false discoveries. Require: unseen data, multiple markets, multiple years, shrinkage-adjusted strength — the existing `overfit-validation-pipeline` doc is precisely this doctrine.
11. **Shrinkage.** Estimate every edge conservatively; if it only works at the optimistic estimate, it isn't there.
12. **One blended model, netted execution.** Blending 100 weak signals beats any single strong one; netting opposite signals cuts costs ~90% in the buy-1000/sell-800 example. Ensemble + netting should be evaluated in our strategy composition too.
13. **State estimation.** The 1964 IDA idea — prices as an HMM with hidden "moods" (quiet/stormy), Baum–Welch/EM to learn them, and **size to the inferred state** — is the same job as our regime/vol filters, formalized.
14. **Frequency slicing.** Laufer's move — split the day into 5-minute slices instead of daily bars — multiplies data (and testable bets) per calendar day. Already our native resolution; the lesson is to exploit *intraday cross-time* patterns (Friday AM→PM, late-day→next open, cross-contract co-reversion).

### C. Risk & business design
15. **Crowding is a risk factor.** Monitor how crowded your signal book is; crowded + leveraged = forced-unwind contagion (Aug 2007). Diversify across uncorrelated signal families.
16. **Separate signal risk from counterparty risk.** Models trade; humans audit *who* holds the money.
17. **Capacity honesty with capital.** Don't run short-horizon alpha on long-horizon-sized capital — the two-clock split (Medallion +76% vs RIEF −19% in 2020) is the empirical proof. If the strategy is scalping, keep it sized like scalping.
18. **Align incentives with ownership.** Insiders only, high fees to your own firm, bonus pool = half of net income, one shared model = no strategy fiefdoms.
19. **Regulatory/tax structures are a risk position.** The basket options bought 15 years of tax savings and a $7B settlement + public storm. Avoid structures whose entire value is label-shifting.

### D. What the video does NOT give you (honesty clause)
- Medallion's actual signals are secret; everything here is reconstruction from Zuckerman, Cornell, the Senate record, Magerman interviews, Patterson talks.
- "50.75%" is an informal Mercer quote, not an audited number. The "1,300 winning days" clip is about **Virtu**, not Renaissance.
- The video's post-2024 figures (2024 +30%, Oct 2025 −15%, RIEF AUM) are as-reported, not audited.
- **Take the principles, not the myth.** The repeatable parts are the boring ones: data hygiene, multiple-testing discipline, Kelly sizing, breadth, capacity honesty. That's the actual moneymaker — and it's all portable to a one-person scalping operation.
- Mid-video segment (~24:00–27:00) is a paid community promo (The Financial Syndicate); excluded from analysis.

---

## 10. One-line summary

> Medallion won because it treated trading as an inference problem: find tiny, real edges, prove them with enormous breadth, size them with Kelly, defend them against self-deception, hedge out the market, take the other side of forced flow, and never ask a signal to carry more capital than its time-scale can bear.

**Follow-up:** seven concrete, pre-registered experiments mapped to our
stack live in `docs/research/medallion-ideas-2026-10-07.md` (breadth audit,
cell-edge Kelly sizing, chip blending, NQ/ES residual, forced-flow capture
cells, HMM state inference, capacity/decay/FDR process items).

# Next Word, Next Tick — deep research on the scalping ⇄ next-token-prediction analogy (2026-10-10)

**The question:** is scalping structurally the same problem as predicting the
next word in speech? Predicting the next word is much easier than predicting
the whole sentence/topic; predicting the next short-term price move is said to
be much easier than predicting the long-term path. Deep research verdict:
**the analogy is true in form, true in the horizon direction, and dangerous in
magnitude** — and the refined version of it (predictability lives in
high-constraint contexts, not in the unconditional stream) is already visible
in our own archive.

**Status:** research note. No code changes, no env changes, nothing shipped.
Raw subagent reports were consolidated into this file and removed from the
repo root.

## 1. The claim, formalized

Let `w_t` be the t-th word (token) of an utterance and `x_t` the t-th price
observation. The user's claim decomposes into three sub-claims:

1. **Same problem shape.** Both tasks are conditional next-step prediction:
   estimate `P(w_t | w_{<t})` vs. estimate `P(x_{t+1} | X_{≤t})`.
2. **Local > global.** The one-step conditional is far easier than the
   long-horizon conditional in both domains: `P(w_t | context)` is easy while
   `P(sentence/topic)` is hard; `P(next move | tape)` is easy while
   `P(day path)` is hard.
3. **Compounding is the mechanism.** The long-horizon prediction is the
   iterated one-step prediction (`k`-fold autoregressive rollout), and errors
   compound with `k`.

All three sub-claims are formalizable, and each has a different verdict.

---

## 2. The shared skeleton — where the analogy is formally correct

Both domains are autoregressive sequence-modeling problems, and they share
real structure:

| Concept | Language | Markets |
|---|---|---|
| Stream | tokens `w_1..w_T` | observations `x_1..x_T` (ticks, bars) |
| Local objective | `P(w_t \| w_{<t})` — next-token cross-entropy | `P(x_{t+1} \| X_{≤t})` — next-move likelihood |
| Local surprise | surprisal `−log P(w_t \| w_{<t})` (N400 / reading time) | the innovation: realized move minus conditional expectation; squared innovation = local volatility |
| Global objective | sentence/topic/plan | the `k`-step path distribution |
| Rollout | autoregressive decoding, error compounding (exposure bias) | variance compounding: for a near-martingale, mean drift ~`k`·μ but noise ~`σ√k` |
| Compression ⇄ prediction | entropy rate, redundancy | entropy rate of returns; predictability = compressibility |
| Quality → money | — | Kelly: edge/growth = information rate (see §5) |

**Why "long horizon is harder" is *generically* true in markets.** For any
near-martingale price process the signal-to-noise ratio of a `k`-step-ahead
conditional mean decays like `1/√k` (drift scales with `k`, noise with `√k`),
while the one-step SNR is the same at every `t`. So *next-step prediction is
mechanically the least-hard prediction problem* in any market — the user's
core intuition has a solid formal core. The same holds in language via error
compounding: each decoded token is conditioned on model-generated tokens
after the first, so rollout error grows with length (exposure bias).

**But the analogy is about *constants*, not just form.** The real question is
not whether both problems have this shape (they do) but how *easy* the
one-step problem is in each domain in absolute terms. Sections 3–5 answer
that; the short version is that language one-step prediction is genuinely easy
(high redundancy, exogenous cooperative generator, trillions of near-iid
samples, errors free) while market one-step prediction is hard in absolute
terms and merely "least hard" relative to the long horizon.

## 3. Language side: how easy is next-word prediction, really?

**Very easy — quantifiably so, and *because* the generator cooperates.**

### 3.1 The founding measurement (Shannon 1951)

Shannon's letter-guessing game
(["Prediction and Entropy of Printed English", BSTJ 30(1):50–64](https://www.princeton.edu/~wbialek/rome/refs/shannon_51.pdf)):
a subject guessing the next letter of literary English is right on the
first guess **69–77%** of the time; with 100 letters of context, **80%**;
with no context, 18.2%. His entropy bounds for printed English: **0.6–1.3
bits/character** against log₂27 ≈ 4.76 max — "something of the order of one
bit per letter, with a corresponding **redundancy of roughly 75%**." The
n-gram ladder collapses fast: F₀=4.70 → F₁=4.14 → F₂=3.56 → F₃=3.3 →
F_word=2.62 bits/letter. Word-level Zipf's law: "the" alone is 7.1% of
tokens, pₙ ≈ k/n, unigram word entropy 11.82 bits/word. The gambling
estimator ([Cover & King 1978, IEEE TIT 24(4)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1055912))
confirms it: **1.34 bits/char**. Notably, machine models are *worse*:
trigram upper bound 1.75 bits/char ([Brown et al. 1992](https://aclanthology.org/J92-1002.pdf)),
LZ-based 1.77 ([Kontoyiannis 1997](https://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/~ik355/PAPERS/english.pdf))
— humans beat local Markov models because they exploit semantics and
long-range structure. Shannon located the residual errors precisely: word
and phrase beginnings, "where the line of thought has more possibility of
branching out."

**Units correction to the original intuition:** the verified human-scale
numbers are bits per **character** (0.6–1.34). Bits per *word* are 5–12
(Shannon unigram 11.82). Model numbers: GPT-2-1.5B LAMBADA ≈ 3.11
bits/word; GPT-3-175B few-shot 0.94 bits/word (86.4% acc)
([Brown et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165)); scaling-law
projected entropy-per-token L* ≈ 2.45 bits ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)).

### 3.2 Why it is tractable — and that humans literally run this predictor

The Markov assumption — the future is predictable from a short window —
captures most of the structure: WSJ perplexity collapses 962 (unigram) →
170 (bigram) → 109 (trigram)
([Jurafsky & Martin, SLP3 ch. 3](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/3.pdf)).
Surprisal theory formalizes local difficulty as −log P(word | context)
([Hale 2001](https://aclanthology.org/N01-1021.pdf);
[Levy 2008](http://www.mit.edu/~rplevy/papers/levy-2008-cognition.pdf)).
The psycholinguistic evidence that the brain *is* a next-word model: N400
amplitude tracks semantic incongruity
([Kutas & Hillyard 1980](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7350657/)) and is
graded by cloze probability ([DeLong et al. 2005](https://www.nature.com/articles/nn1504) —
though the article pre-activation effect failed a 9-lab replication while
the noun effect held, [Nieuwland et al. 2018](https://elifesciences.org/articles/33468));
reading time is logarithmic in predictability
([Smith & Levy 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0010027713000413)).
In the direct head-to-head, **humans score 29–30% top-1 next-token accuracy
vs GPT-3's 56%** — "even small LMs are superhuman at next-token prediction"
([Goldstein et al. 2022, arXiv:2212.11281](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.11281)).
And across 17 languages humans transmit at a nearly constant ~39 bits/s —
predictability is partly *manufactured* by cooperative speakers for the
listener ([Coupé et al. 2019, Sci. Adv. 5](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aaw2594)).

### 3.3 Local → global: the composition theorem and its failure modes

The chain rule makes the sequence likelihood a **sum** of one-step terms,
and the KL chain rule says small average per-step divergence keeps the joint
distribution close — that is why purely local training produces long fluent
outputs ([Cover & Thomas, Thm 2.5.3](https://cs-114.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/Elements_of_Information_Theory_Elements.pdf);
[GPT-2](https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf)).
But the path is not determined: at H bits/step there are 2^H plausible
continuations per step, so P(exact n-step match) ≈ (1−ε)ⁿ ≈ e^(−nε) —
Shannon's excellent 80%-per-letter subject reproduces a 100-letter passage
exactly with probability ~10⁻¹⁰. The failure modes match this arithmetic:
exposure bias with worst-case **Tε ≤ R ≤ T²ε** accumulation, measured
near-quadratically on GPT-2 ([Arora et al. 2022](https://aclanthology.org/2022.findings-acl.58.pdf));
self-reinforcing repetition under likelihood-maximizing decoding
([Holtzman et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751));
early-error compounding on compositional chains
([Dziri et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18654));
and the long-range tail — LAMBADA items are exactly those guessable from
the whole passage but *not* from the last sentence alone, where 2016 LMs
scored <1% vs GPT-3's 86.4%
([Paperno et al. 2016](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1606.06031)).

**This side's honest verdict:** local prediction in language is easy
(0.6–1.34 bits/char, 69–80% first-guess) *precisely because the generator
cooperates* — a speaker optimizes to be predictable; global path prediction
is exponentially harder, and its difficulty lives at branch points and
long-range dependencies. Whether the price process has a cooperative
generator is the market-side question — and §4's answer is that it does
not.

## 4. Market side: is the next tick actually easier than the next month?

**Direct answer:** in the sense the analogy needs (a monotone difficulty
gradient — "next word easy, next paragraph hard") **no**. In a narrow,
economically-thin statistical sense (more directional predictability per
event at tick scale than at monthly scale) **yes — but it is almost entirely
microstructure, and it barely survives costs.**

### 4.1 The theory pins the best forecast at "no change" at every horizon

Bachelier (1900) stated the fair-game principle ("the mathematical
expectation of the speculator is zero"; deviations ∝ √t —
[French original](https://www.numdam.org/item/10.24033/asens.476.pdf);
[English translation](http://radio.goldseek.com/bachelier-thesis-theory-of-speculation-en.pdf));
Samuelson (1965) proved that properly anticipated prices follow a martingale
`E[P(t+1)|Φ(t)] = P(t)`; Fama (1970) measured daily serial correlations of
30 DJIA stocks at mostly −0.12…+0.12, ρ=0.06 ⇒ R² = **0.36%** — "unlikely
that the small absolute levels of serial correlation … can be used as the
basis of substantially profitable trading systems"
([Fama 1970 full-text scan](http://www.e-m-h.org/Fama70.pdf)). The martingale
says expected excess profit is ~zero at **every** horizon — it does not
predict a "short is easier" gradient. Unlike language, the short horizon is
not where theory says entropy is lowest.

### 4.2 The autocorrelation structure is non-monotone — the sign flips

The horizon profile from tick to decade is not a decay curve:

| Horizon | Autocorrelation sign | Magnitude | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| tick (pure bounce) | **negative** | ρ1 → −0.5 (Cov = −s²/4) | [Roll 1984 model; Fed WP 2019-051](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/files/2019051pap.pdf) |
| daily | ≈ 0 | −0.12…+0.12 | [Fama 1970](http://www.e-m-h.org/Fama70.pdf) |
| weekly | **positive** | VR(2) = 1.30 EW (~30%) / 1.08 VW (~8%) | [Lo & MacKinlay 1988](https://www.nber.org/papers/w2168) |
| monthly (individual stocks) | **negative** | decile contrarian 2.49%/mo | [Jegadeesh 1990](https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v45y1990i3p881-98.html) |
| 3–12 months | **positive** (momentum) | **12.01%/yr** (6/6) | [Jegadeesh & Titman 1993](https://www.bauer.uh.edu/rsusmel/phd/jegadeesh-titman93.pdf) |
| 3–8 years | **negative** | VR(96 mo) = 0.54; 25–45% of 3–5-y variance predictable | [Poterba & Summers 1988](https://www.nber.org/papers/w2343); [Fama & French 1988](http://www.e-m-h.org/FaFr88.pdf) |

Predictability does **not** decay monotonically from short to long — it
changes sign repeatedly, and the largest *economically significant* anomalies
(momentum, long-run reversal) sit at months-to-years. The raw autocorrelation
evidence supports "short = noise-dominated, with a thin microstructure
component," not "short = more predictable."

### 4.3 Where the tick-level signal actually lives

- Order-flow imbalance explains **R² = 65%** of 10-second mid-price changes
  across 50 NYSE stocks (volume: 6%), impact β ∝ 1/depth
  ([Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.6402)).
- DeepLOB: next-move accuracy **78.9% / F1 77.7%** at 10-event horizon on
  FI-2010 (classical baselines: 48–86% accuracy but F1 only 36–47% — class
  imbalance inflates accuracy); on real LSE data accuracy **decays with
  horizon: 70.2% (k=20) → 63.9% (k=50) → 61.5% (k=100)**
  ([arXiv:1808.03668](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.03668)).
- Sirignano & Cont 2019: DL beats linear models by 5–10% for next-move
  direction (event time, ~1.7 s, 50% baseline); stable 18 months OOS;
  absolute accuracy only in figures (~65–68% per common citations —
  **unverified**)
  ([arXiv:1803.06917](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.06917)).
- Avellaneda & Stoikov 2008: the market maker's edge is **inventory-risk
  pricing**, not direction forecasting
  ([NYU PDF](https://www.math.nyu.edu/faculty/avellane/HighFrequencyTrading.pdf)).

**The killer caveat:** DeepLOB's own trading simulation uses mid-prices
*without transaction costs* — the authors concede that is "not a reasonable
assumption for a standalone strategy." A large share of the impressive
tick-level accuracy *is the bid-ask bounce itself* (ρ1 → −0.5), whose
expected value equals the spread you pay to harvest it.

### 4.4 The economics: the edge is real and ≈ equal to its cost

- Grossman–Stiglitz: the equilibrium is "an equilibrium degree of
  disequilibrium" — prices are inefficient only up to the amount that
  compensates information acquisition ([AER 70(3), p. 393](https://www.aeaweb.org/aer/top20/70.3.393-408.pdf)).
- The measured short-horizon economy matches: HFT firms earn **median
  annualized Sharpe 4.30** (p90: 12.68) but **$0.46 median profit per E-mini
  contract** ([Baron et al. 2019](https://www.cftc.gov/sites/default/files/idc/groups/public/@economicanalysis/documents/file/oce_riskandreturn0414.pdf));
  ES–SPY mechanical arbitrage ≈ 800 opportunities/day ≈ $75M/yr, and market
  wide latency rents ≈ **$5B/yr** — *speed* rents funded by wider spreads
  ([Budish, Cramton & Shim 2015](https://images.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/AQR-Insight-Award/2014/TheHighFrequencyTradingArmsRace.pdf);
  [Aquilina, Budish & O'Neill 2022](https://www.nber.org/papers/w29011)).
- Cost anchors: access-fee cap $0.003/share; effective spread ~3 bps; an ES
  tick ≈ 0.4 bp. A tick-level directional edge of ~1 tick per trade is the
  same order as the spread it must cross.
- Zero-cost backtests "ruin any attempt to produce a reliable backtest"
  ([Briola et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2403.09267v1));
  the only located net-of-cost positive result is a slower Chinese A-share
  market ([Yin & Wong 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0957417422019170)).
  Net-of-cost profitability of LOB deep learning in fast Western markets is
  **not established** in any located peer-reviewed study.

### 4.5 The explicit tick-as-language analogy exists — as architecture transfer

Treating order-book messages as a language is an established methodological
move: LOBERT 2025 ("treating the stream of LOB events as a unique language,"
BERT-style masked modeling — [arXiv:2511.12563](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12563));
Nagy et al. 2023 (token-level autoregressive LOB model, evaluated with
perplexity — [arXiv:2309.00638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00638));
ByteGen 2025 ([arXiv:2508.02247](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02247));
MarketGPT 2024 ([arXiv:2411.16585](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.16585)).
Practitioner version: "the models themselves don't really care if the
sequences are about words or limit order book messages"
([ai-street.co](https://www.ai-street.co/p/treating-trading-data-as-language)).
**But no located source claims tick prediction is *as easy* as next-word
prediction or quantifies a difficulty gradient** — that premise of the
analogy has no literature support. Quant Memo's summary of Sirignano–Cont
states the key caveat: "the move you have predicted is often smaller than
the bid-ask spread… High directional accuracy and zero trading profit are
entirely compatible"
([quantmemo.com](https://quantmemo.com/writing/paper-sirignano-cont-universal-price-formation)).

## 5. The information-theoretic bridge: prediction ⇄ betting

The analogy is not just evocative — it is a **theorem-level mapping**. The
bridge was built by Shannon's Bell Labs colleague John Kelly in 1956, and it
is exactly the identity that turns "how good is my next-symbol model" into
"how fast does my money grow".

### 5.1 Kelly 1956: growth rate = information rate

Kelly's setup: a gambler bets on events and receives a noisy "private wire"
signal `Y` about the outcome `X` before betting. His theorem: the maximum
exponential growth rate `G*` of the gambler's capital equals Shannon's
transmission rate — `G* = R = H(X) − H(X|Y) = I(X;Y)`. In his words, *"the
maximum exponential rate of growth of the gambler's capital is equal to the
rate of transmission of information over the channel."*
([Kelly 1956, BSTJ 35:917–926](https://masters.donntu.ru/2009/fvti/kravchenko/library/article2.htm);
[IEEE record](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1056803)).
Two load-bearing details: betting all-in maximizes *arithmetic* expectation
but ruins you with probability 1, and the log-optimal (Kelly) bettor
asymptotically dominates every other fixed fraction — which is why prediction
quality maps to **log** growth, not arithmetic growth. (This is the formal
backing for the repo's Kelly mode, §7 of `kelly-mode-2026-10-07.md`.)

### 5.2 The identity: cross-entropy IS the trading objective

Cover & Thomas's "horse race" form generalizes Kelly: bet fractions `b(x)`
on outcome `x` at posted odds `o(x)`, expected log-wealth rate
`W(b) = Σ p(x)·log(b(x)·o(x))`. Three consequences
([Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, Ch. 6](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/0471200611.ch6)):

- Bet proportional to the truth `p`: `W(p) = Σ p log o − H(p)`.
- Side information adds exactly the mutual information: `ΔW = I(X;Y)` —
  every bit of genuine predictive information is one bit of extra log-growth
  per event.
- **Bet with a wrong model `q`: `W(q) = Σ p log o − H(p,q)`** — expected log
  growth = (log odds) − (your cross-entropy), and each bit of model error
  costs `D(p‖q)` bits of log-growth per event.

So the cross-entropy a language model minimizes is, up to an additive odds
constant, **literally the negative log-growth rate of a Kelly bettor using
that model.** Next-word training loss and log-optimal scalping P&L are the
same functional. The scalping mapping item by item:

| LM concept | Scalping concept |
|---|---|
| token `w_t` | next price increment, or an ordinal pattern of the last `m` returns (Bandt–Pompe symbolization — "the alphabet of price movements") |
| `P(w_t \| w_{<t})` | `P(r_{t+1} \| order book, tape)` — exactly the DeepLOB/deepVOL cross-entropy setup |
| training loss = cross-entropy `H(p,q)` | P&L ceiling per bar = `I(future; past)` bits, minus costs |
| perplexity `2^H(p,q)` | exp(−growth rate) of the corresponding Kelly bettor |
| size = fixed | size = Kelly fraction `f* = edge/odds` |

### 5.3 Why "local beats long-horizon" is formally true in both

The entropy rate `h = lim H(X_{n+1} | X_1..X_n)` is the *same* limit whether
you predict one step or the whole future — but an `h`-step forecast is the
product of `h` one-step conditionals, so any per-step modeling error
compounds across `h` (in language: exposure bias; in markets: bet held across
`h` bars of noise and cost). Next-step prediction has minimal accumulated
divergence in both domains. The formal machinery is identical.

### 5.4 The regime contrast: how many bits are actually there?

This is where the analogy's magnitude shows itself:

- **Language:** Shannon's human-guessing experiment bounded English at
  **0.6–1.3 bits/char** against `log₂27 ≈ 4.75` max → **redundancy ~50–75%**
  ([Shannon 1951, "Prediction and Entropy of Printed English"](https://www.nokia.com/bell-labs/publications-and-media/publications/prediction-and-entropy-of-printed-english/));
  Cover & King's gambling estimator: 1.34 bits/char
  ([IEEE TIT 24(4)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/1055912)).
  The *majority* of each next symbol is locally determined by context.
- **Markets:** developed markets cluster **near the maximum-entropy corner**
  of the complexity–entropy causality plane; emerging/inefficient markets sit
  measurably further away with more forbidden ordinal patterns
  ([Zunino et al. 2009, Physica A 388](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physa.2009.03.042);
  [2010, Physica A 389](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378437110000042);
  "commodity markets are not totally efficient. Long-range dependence is
  present" — [2011, Physica A 390](https://digital.csic.es/dspace-oai/request?verb=GetRecord&metadataPrefix=oai_dc&identifier=oai:digital.csic.es:10261/48386)).
  Inter-market transfer entropy is real but small
  ([Marschinski & Kantz 2002](https://epjb.epj.org/articles/epjb/abs/2002/22/b01535/b01535.html);
  US is the dominant source among 25 indices — [Kwon & Yang 2008](https://arxiv.org/abs/0802.1747)).
  At high frequency, next-move predictability is "not just present, but
  ubiquitous" when scored as next-symbol cross-entropy against an IID/EMH
  benchmark ([Lucchese, Pakkanen & Veraart, arXiv:2211.13777](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.13777));
  DeepLOB-class models reach high, transferable next-move accuracy
  ([arXiv:1808.03668](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.03668)).

**One sentence:** language redundancy ≈ 50–75% means most of the next symbol
is context-determined; price series sit *near* max entropy with only thin,
horizon-decaying structure. The harvestable bits per symbol differ by roughly
an order of magnitude — and in markets they arrive already priced by
competition.

### 5.5 Compression = prediction, and "market as language" is mainstream

A source is predictable iff it is compressible (Shannon source-coding
theorem; MDL: [Grünwald 2007](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262072816/the-minimum-description-length-principle/);
Solomonoff: incompressible = maximally unpredictable). A direct EMH
formulation — "an efficient market is one in which the pragmatic information
of the tradable past about current prices is zero" — exists only in a
**withdrawn** preprint ([arXiv:0903.2243](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.2243);
flagged, not an established result). The market-as-language program is now
mainstream: transformer forecasters ([TFT, arXiv:1912.09363](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.09363);
[Stockformer, arXiv:2401.06139](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.06139)) up to
Kronos — a decoder-only autoregressive "K-line language model" whose
tokenizer quantizes OHLCV bars into discrete tokens, trained on 45+ exchanges
([arXiv:2508.02739](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02739)). Shannon's own link to
markets runs through Kelly and his documented practice ("Shannon's Demon" —
50/50 rebalancing to harvest volatility), which is anecdote-level history
([Poundstone, Fortune's Formula, 2005](https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/fortunes-formula-william-poundstone/1100292700)),
not audited data.

### 5.6 The gap that matters for us

There is **no canonical "bits per bar" number** for any standard index in
open literature — language has 0.6–1.3 bits/char, finance has only
permutation-entropy proxies. That missing measurement is computable on our
own archive (§9): the entropy rate of the NQ 1-min stream, the mutual
information `I(future; past)` at bar horizons 1–30, and — most interestingly
— the **conditional entropy inside signal states vs. outside them**, which
would measure the "idiom effect" of §7 directly in bits.
